activity: to plan a week of meals, shop for the ingredients and cook them in batches
knowledge_domain: to plan a week of meals, shop for the ingredients and cook them in batches
fact: The USDA calls 4 to 60 degrees Celsius (40 to 140 degrees Fahrenheit) the danger zone, the range where bacteria in food multiply rapidly.
story:
Jaxon stood in Misha's kitchen on Sunday afternoon with a printed spreadsheet and a pen he kept tucking behind his ear and losing. The spreadsheet had columns for Monday through Friday, for lunch and dinner, and it was the most organized thing he had ever made, which Misha pointed out every ten minutes or so. "You color-coded lentils," Misha said, leaning over his shoulder. "You gave legumes their own color."

"Lentils are cheap and they keep," Jaxon said. "This is called strategy." His mother had shipped him a care package the week before with a note that read, in her insouciant scrawl, "You cannot live on vending machines, love, Mum," which was rich coming from a woman who once served birthday cake for dinner. But she worked nights now, and the house was quieter, and somebody had to figure out the food. He had volunteered mostly to prove he could, and partly because he was tired of cereal at 9 p.m. with the guilty concentration of a raccoon.

Misha's kitchen was the classroom because Misha's parents had a chest freezer and an actual stockpot, and because Misha, unlike Francesco, did not narrate everything like a nature documentary. Francesco arrived anyway, carrying a bag of tortilla chips as tuition. "I'm here to supervise," he announced. "And to eat."

They batch-cooked. Jaxon browned two kilograms of ground turkey while Misha chopped an unreasonable quantity of onions, and Francesco read the recipe aloud in a robot voice until Misha threatened him with a wooden spoon. By evening they had five containers of chili, a tray of baked chicken thighs, a pot of rice, and the smug exhaustion of people who had planned something and then actually done it. Jaxon labeled everything with masking tape. He was still awake at midnight when the last container went into the fridge, and that was the moment he should have paid attention to, except there was one pot left, the biggest one, still steaming on the stove, and Misha said leave it, it'll cool faster out here, and Jaxon, whose understanding of cooling was a household adage rather than a fact, agreed and went home to bed.

The flashback that haunted him on Monday morning was small and specific: his grandfather, years ago, lifting a pot of soup off the stove at the lake cabin and setting it on the porch overnight because that was how it had always been done. Everyone had eaten it the next day and been fine. Jaxon had been maybe nine, and he remembered the steam rising off the porch boards like the pot was breathing. He had thought of it as wisdom. Now, sitting in first period, he thought of it as luck, and the distinction bothered him all the way through chemistry.

After school he went back to Misha's to collect his share of the haul. The big pot sat on the stove exactly where they had left it, lid on, twelve hours gone. Misha lifted the lid and inhaled. "Smells fine," he said, reaching for a spoon.

"Don't," Jaxon said, and then, because he sounded like a cautionary pamphlet, he pulled out his phone. He had looked it up during lunch, hunched over the table while Francesco stole his fries, and the words were still open on the screen. "The USDA calls 4 to 60 degrees Celsius the danger zone. That's 40 to 140 Fahrenheit. It's the range where bacteria in food multiply rapidly." He turned the phone around. "It sat out all night. Room temperature is inside that."

Misha squinted at the screen. "So the whole night, it was just, what, marinating in bacteria?"

"Basically a spa for bacteria," Francesco said from the doorway, where he had appeared with chips again, like a seagull.

"Okay," Misha said slowly, "but my grandpa left soup out all the time and nobody died."

"I know," Jaxon said. "Mine too." And that was the part he couldn't resolve, standing in the bright kitchen with the pot between them. His grandfather's porch soup had fed a family and become a story. This pot had sat through the same hours and smelled fine and might be perfectly safe or might not, and there was no way to taste the difference. He tried to allay his own doubt by reading the page a second time, but the page only told him where the risk lived, not whether it had moved in.

They tipped the chili into the compost pail. It went with a wet, regretful sound, and Misha said a small eulogy, "You were delicious in theory," and Francesco saluted with a tortilla chip. Jaxon scraped the pot clean and rewrote the top line of his spreadsheet in pen: cool it in shallow containers, fridge within two hours, do not trust the porch. Then he took his four surviving containers, still cold from the freezer bag, and paused at the door.

"Same time next Sunday?" Misha asked. "I'll buy the onions."

"Buy extra," Jaxon said. "We clearly need supervision and a better system."

"You're the system guy now," Francesco called after him. "The lentil color-coding system guy."

Jaxon flipped him off with both hands full of chili and walked out into the cold.

activity: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
knowledge_domain: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
fact: A Marxist reading often asks whose labour makes the characters' comfortable lives possible, noticing servants and workers the novel mentions only in passing.
story:
Rosalie arrived at the book club with two novels, a pencil she had chewed down to the wood, and a notebook page covered in tally marks. The club met in the back room of the secondhand bookshop on Halloran Street, where Mr. Lewandowski moved the cardboard boxes off the folding chairs every second Thursday and set out a plate of ginger biscuits nobody ever finished. She took her usual seat near the radiator, which ticked like something counting.

They were halfway through Emma this month. Domenic had claimed the opening chapters, and he read his prepared remarks from his phone, pausing occasionally to let everyone appreciate him. He was twelve minutes in when Rosalie noticed he had not once mentioned the people carrying the trays.

"Could I add something?" she said, and immediately regretted the smallness of her voice, so she said it again, louder. "I counted."

Domenic lowered his phone. "Counted what?"

"The servants. In the volume we read." She turned her notebook toward the circle of chairs. The page showed two columns of strokes, one much shorter than the other, the ink smudged where her thumb had rested. "They're mentioned, by my count, over and over, and they speak... almost never. I went through it twice, because I thought I'd made a mistake. Somebody makes Hartfield run. Somebody cooks, somebody carries letters, somebody lights the fires before anyone wakes up. And they have no lines. The whole picnic, the whole dinner party, it's all resting on them, and the novel just... passes over them." She heard her own voice accelerate and made herself slow down. "I was trying a Marxist reading. A Marxist reading often asks whose labour makes the characters' comfortable lives possible."

The radiator ticked into the silence. Mr. Lewandowski, who owned the shop and had started the club the year his wife died, reached for a biscuit and then didn't take one.

"That's a bit grim, though," Cassius said. He was curled sideways in his chair, boots on the rung, and he alone had read the whole novel already, twice, which he never let anyone forget. "It's a comedy. Emma's going to be fine. Everybody ends up married and rich. Do you want to read a book about footmen?"

"I want to read a book where the footman gets a name." She felt the blush climb her neck. "That's the point, isn't it? The comfort looks natural to us because the novel never shows us its cost. The floor is always warm. Nobody ever splits the wood."

Domenic, who had been waiting with visible patience for his turn to resume, said, "Look, you can read anything into anything if you try hard enough. That's extrinsic to the text. The author didn't intend it."

"Intention is a weird place to hide," Rosalie said, and was surprised at herself. She had planned nothing; the sentence had simply been there. "The servants are in the sentences. Whether she thought about them or not, they're in there, doing the work."

Cassius sat up, which he did only when genuinely interested. "All right, but here's my problem with your tally. It's not wrong, exactly. It's just that you're reducing the book to its furniture. One footman standing for the whole economy, every servant a little synecdoche. And then you stop seeing the actual people on the page, Emma and her father and Miss Bates, who is one bad quarter away from being a servant herself."

The radiator ticked. Rosalie looked at her smudged columns and found that she could not decide, in that moment, whether Cassius had just dismantled her reading or improved it. Miss Bates chattered through every scene, and Rosalie had counted her as gentry, had counted her as one of the comfortable ones, and that was wrong, or partly wrong, or wrong in a way that mattered. "Maybe both things are true," she said slowly. "The counting shows you something the novel hides. And the counting can hide something the novel shows. I don't know which one I'm supposed to trust."

"Nobody said trust," Mr. Lewandowski said. It was the first thing he had said all evening, and the room turned toward him like plants toward a window. "Choose a page for next time. Any page. Read it your way and then against your way." He stood and began stacking the untouched biscuits back into their tin. "And Domenic, if you pontificate past the hour mark again, I'm charging rent."

Outside, the street was cold enough that their breath hung in front of them, and Domenic walked off toward the bus stop still arguing that authorial intent settled it. Cassius fell into step beside Rosalie and asked, without looking at her, which page she'd choose. She held up the notebook, tally marks showing through the streetlight's orange wash. "The one where the fire gets lit," she said, and turned the page toward him so he could see where she'd stopped counting.

activity: to compare how a parliamentary and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government
knowledge_domain: to compare how a parliamentary and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government
fact: In the United States, the House of Representatives impeaches a president by a simple majority, but the Senate needs a two-thirds vote to convict and remove them.
story:
Austin spread his notes across his grandfather's kitchen table, where the plastic cloth had printed roosters on it and the afternoon light came through the lace curtains in bars. His grandfather was in the other room watching a parliamentary channel, volume low, and Austin could hear the murmur of question period the way you hear rain on a car roof. He had a quiz Monday on how different countries pick and fire their leaders, and he had two systems in front of him that refused to sit still next to each other.

The parliamentary side was easier to hold in his head. The party that wins the most seats picks the prime minister from among its own members, and if the party stops supporting that person, the leader can fall without any election at all. A vote of no confidence, a leadership challenge, and the head of government was simply gone, replaced by someone from the same parliament. It was like the class choosing a lab partner and then quietly choosing someone else the next day if the first one broke the beakers.

The presidential side had seemed just as simple until last week, when his class had toured the county courthouse and a boy in front had asked the guide whether a president who got impeached had to leave office. The guide, a volunteer with a laminated badge, had shaken her head. "People mix that up all the time," she said. "In the United States, the House of Representatives impeaches a president by a simple majority, but the Senate needs a two-thirds vote to convict and remove them." Austin had written it on his hand in the parking lot and copied it into his notebook that night, and now it sat in the middle of his page like a stone in a stream, making the water go around it.

Layla arrived at four with her bike helmet still buckled to her backpack and a bag of plums from the tree in her yard. She dropped into the chair opposite him and pulled his notes toward her without asking. "You're doing the systems thing," she said. "Tiana wants me to tell her it's basically the same everywhere with different accents."

"It's not." Austin took a plum and turned it over. "That's what I keep getting wrong in my head. I keep wanting one of them to be the easy one." He told her about the courthouse, repeating what the guide had said, and watched Layla frown at the word two-thirds.

"So a majority of one house can charge him," she said slowly, "and then you need way more than a majority of the other house to actually throw him out." She bit into her plum. "That's like a teacher writing you up but the principal needing almost everybody in the building to agree before you're suspended."

"Right," Austin said, and then stopped, because he realized the comparison he'd been reaching for all afternoon had just been handed to him. In a parliament, removal was ordinary, a matter of colleagues withdrawing support; in the American system, removal was deliberately hard, a bar set high enough that charging a president and removing one were two separate events. He said this out loud, half to Layla and half to the roosters on the tablecloth, and Layla said it sounded right, though she was already texting Tiana.

His grandfather came in for his tea and stood behind Austin's chair, reading the page upside down with the sullen patience of a man who believed anything worth learning had been available in his day for free. He pointed at Austin's paragraph about votes of no confidence and said, "That's how we lost Bennett," and when Austin asked who that was, his grandfather waved the question away and went back to the kettle, leaving Austin to decide whether the anecdote had been a gift or an affectation of toughness he performed for company. Either way, Austin wrote Bennett in the margin with a question mark, because he didn't want to lose the thread.

By the time Layla left, the bars of light had moved across the table and Austin had drawn a diagram with two columns, one for each system, arrows showing how a leader could rise and fall. The parliamentary column had short arrows. The presidential column had one arrow that ended at a high wall marked two-thirds. He still couldn't say which system was fairer; fairness seemed to depend on whether you feared a government that could be toppled in an afternoon or one that couldn't be toppled at all. He ate the last plum and looked at the two columns until the words blurred. In the other room, the parliament was still murmuring, and someone was being told, sharply, to take his seat.

activity: applying to college and waiting for the answer
knowledge_domain: applying to college and waiting for the answer
fact: The SAT switched to a digital, adaptive format in the United States in March 2024: how well a student does on the first module of each section sets the difficulty of the second.
story:
The portal had been open for six minutes, and Lea had not clicked the button. Her cursor hovered over "View Application Status" the way a foot hovers over ice you already suspect is thin. The kitchen was quiet except for the refrigerator, and outside the window the March light lay flat on the neighbor's fence, on the strip of creek behind it, on the riparian tangle of willow and cane that she had looked at every morning of her life without once thinking she might miss it.

She thought of texting Tegan, who had checked her own decision at 8:01, but Tegan's silence since then was its own kind of information. Instead Lea did what she had done all winter when she couldn't stand her own head: she opened her messages and scrolled back to October, to the test.

The morning of the digital SAT, she had gone in confident, the way you can only be confident before anything has happened. The first math module had felt almost easy, and then the second had opened like a trapdoor. Question after question she didn't recognize, problems that seemed to belong to some other, faster student. She had finished the section with her hand shaking on the mouse, certain she had bombed it, and had walked out past Ms. Somsak, who was collecting scratch paper in the hallway, without being able to say anything at all.

She hadn't told anyone the score until Tegan cornered her at the lockers the day results came out. "You got a 740 in math," Tegan had said, reading the screen over her shoulder before Lea could angle it away. "That's basically perfect. What is your face doing."

"Because the second module was impossible," Lea had said. "It was all questions I'd never seen."

"Okay, so, it's adaptive," Tegan said. "The SAT switched to that in March. Digital, adaptive. However you do on the first module sets the difficulty of the second one." Lea had stared at her. "So if your second module was brutal," Tegan went on, "that might mean you did well enough on the first to earn the hard one. It's not a punishment. It's a ladder." Lea had wanted to argue, to say that a test shouldn't be a riddle about itself, but the number on the screen kept insisting otherwise. Hard questions as a reward: it had taken her days to stop resenting how much she liked that idea.

She closed the messages now and looked at the button again. It occurred to her, with a small cold clarity, that admissions might work the same way, that everything in her life recently had been a first module she couldn't see the scoring of. The essay she had revised eleven times. The deferred decision from December, the email that said "we remain interested," which she had read as a polite refusal and her mother had read as hope and Savana had read, characteristically, as "bureaucratic flirting."

Her phone buzzed. Savana: "TEGAN GOT IN. She's crying in the parking lot of the Bagel Barn. Are you alive. Did you check. Do not make me drive over there and beseech you through the window like a Victorian."

Lea typed "checking now," set the phone face down, and put her hand on the mouse. She thought about Savana, who had applied nowhere, who was taking a gap year to work on her uncle's boat and considered the whole application process a superstition. She thought about Ms. Somsak, who once told the class that good judgment, real discernment, was mostly the willingness to look at a thing you'd already decided about and check it again. Lea had written that down in a notebook and then never opened the notebook. She was opening something now, which she chose to count.

The page loaded in pieces: the college seal, a line of small print, then a single block of text in the center of the screen. She read the first sentence twice, because the first sentence contained the word "congratulations" and she did not trust her own eyes to deliver it accurately. Behind the word, arriving late, was everything it cost: the creek out the window, the bedroom she'd painted sophomore year, Tegan crying in a parking lot forty minutes away, Savana on her boat next fall, all of it suddenly on the other side of a fact.

She picked up the phone. Before she could dial, it buzzed again: Tegan, this time, actual calling. Lea looked at the screen, at her name, at the window where the willows were already budding green, and answered. "So," Tegan said, her voice wrecked and laughing at once. "Which module did you get?"

activity: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
knowledge_domain: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
fact: Emergency contraceptive pills work mainly by delaying ovulation, and they are more effective the sooner they are taken after unprotected sex.
story:
The text came at 9:40 on a Tuesday, while Maya was highlighting her chemistry notes: "can you come with me. please don't ask why yet." Braden never said please. She wrote back that she'd meet him outside the pharmacy on Caldwell in twenty minutes, then sat for a moment with her pen still resting on the chapter about how atoms ionize when they lose electrons, becoming something slightly other than themselves. She thought of that on the walk over, how a small loss could change what a thing was able to do.

He was standing under the awning with his hands jammed in his jacket pockets, and beside him was a girl Maya recognized vaguely from the sectarian school across town, the one whose students sometimes joined their debate meets. Her name, Braden said quietly, was not important right now. "It was Saturday night," the girl said, staring at the automatic doors. "We used nothing. I keep reading things online and they all say different stuff and I don't know what's still true."

"Saturday," Maya repeated. Three days gone already. She held the door and steered them past the sunscreen display toward the counter at the back, where a pharmacist in a blue coat was counting pills into a tray. His name tag said Mr. Jean-Louis. Maya had met him once before, when her mother sent her for cough syrup and he had asked, without hurry, whether the cough was wet or dry, and waited for a real answer.

The girl couldn't seem to start, so Maya did. "My friend needs emergency contraception," she said, "and she wants to know if it's too late." The girl's shoulders dropped half an inch, as if Maya had taken some weight off them by saying the words out loud.

"It's not too late," Mr. Jean-Louis said, "but you shouldn't wait longer, because it works mainly by delaying ovulation, and it's more effective the sooner you take it." He set down his tray. "The window is a real thing, not a scare tactic." While he rang it up, cheaper than the girl had feared, he asked if she wanted to talk about ongoing contraception, and she said, in a voice steadier than before, yes, actually, she did, and he walked her through the options behind the counter and wrote the name of a clinic on a card. "They do testing for infections there too," he added. "Simple, confidential, you can book online." The girl slid the card into her sleeve like it was something she'd been looking for in a drawer for years.

Outside, Braden walked the girl to her bus, and Maya sat on the bench by the ice cream freezer to wait. She thought about the consent workshop Mr. Jean-Louis's pamphlets had mentioned, the one her own school had run last spring, where a coach had stumbled through a slideshow and everyone had laughed at the wrong moments. At the time Maya had thought it was a box being ticked. Now she thought about the girl saying we used nothing and how many things that phrase could contain, including things the workshop had actually named, things Maya had rolled her eyes at. There was a version of caring that was rules recited in a gymnasium, and a version that was a pharmacist counting out a dose and saying don't wait longer while the clock ran. Maybe they were the same project at different temperatures. She couldn't decide, and she let herself not decide.

When Braden came back, he dropped onto the bench beside her. "She said you didn't ask why," he said. "Even after. She noticed that."

"You can ask me now if you want," Maya said. "But you don't have to."

Braden looked at the pharmacy doors, where a woman was going in with a toddler on her hip. "It's going to be a while before she stops shaking," he said. "Her parents don't know anything about any of this. Not the Saturday part, not the pharmacy part." He rubbed his eyes with the heel of his hand. "The clinic card is in her sleeve and that's the whole plan right now. That's all we've got."

"That's not nothing," Maya said. She pulled her chemistry notes back out of her bag, the diagram of the atom split open, its lone electron sketched flying off in a little arc. "Saturday was three days ago and she took it today. That still counts." Braden nodded slowly, watching a bus turn the corner, and Maya uncapped her highlighter.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: US food safety guidance says perishable food should not sit between 40 and 140 degrees Fahrenheit for more than two hours, or one hour when it is above 90 degrees.
story:
The thermometer clipped to the canopy pole read 94 degrees at four in the afternoon, and Emile had been watching it the way other people watched a pot waiting to boil. The cookout had started before noon. His father had grilled chicken and burgers while Emile handled the sides, and now the family had drifted down to the lake, leaving him with a table of cooling food and a decision he was starting to understand was his alone to make.

The coolers sat in the shade of the poplar at the edge of the site, one still half full of ice, the other holding the drinks. He had learned the rule somewhere, probably from Justina, who had spent a whole unit on food safety in her culinary elective and recited facts at lunch the way other people recited lyrics. Perishable food should not sit between 40 and 140 degrees for more than two hours, she had said, and only one hour when the temperature was above 90. At the time he had filed it away as one more thing she knew. Now he looked at the thermometer again, at the 94, and began counting backward through the afternoon.

The burgers had come off the grill around twelve-thirty. The chicken a little before that. The potato salad his mother had brought up in the morning, the macaroni his aunt had made at home and carried in a covered dish, the sliced tomatoes and the bowl of cut melon. Each item, he realized, had its own clock, and the clocks had not started at the same moment. He stood at the picnic table with his hands on his hips and felt the peculiar weight of being the one who noticed.

He texted Justina first. "Still true that stuff can't sit out more than 2 hours if it's under 90? It's 94 here." She answered within a minute, which meant she was at work with her phone on the counter. "One hour over 90. Two hours below that. Between 40 and 140. Why, are you dying?" He typed "deciding about leftovers" and put the phone face down on the table.

The nearest cooler still had ice, enough to underwrite the whole operation if he moved quickly, though he had to admit the word his economics teacher loved, borrowed for the occasion, sat strangely in his head next to the smell of grilled chicken. He opened the cooler and counted the space. Not enough for everything. The macaroni dish was large and awkward; the melon bowl was worse. He would have to be parsimonious about what he saved, and parsimony, with food, felt like a smaller virtue than it did in a budget.

Emilee came up the path from the lake with wet hair and a towel around her shoulders, because she and her family had the site two over and had joined the cookout around two. "What are you doing up here alone?" she asked, and then she saw the table. "Oh. Is that all still out?"

"It's been out since lunch," Emile said. "It's 94 degrees."

"So is everything garbage now?"

"Not everything. It's been more than an hour, but under two, I think, for most of it. Justina says the cutoff is two hours below 90 and one hour above it, for anything perishable between 40 and 140 degrees. It's a window, and the heat shortens it."

Emilee picked up the thermometer, turned it as if she could bargain with it, and set it back. "So what's under an hour?"

"The melon, maybe. That went out last. The tomatoes." He touched the side of the macaroni dish. Still faintly cool at the base, warm at the rim, which told him nothing he could trust. The chicken and burgers had been out for nearly four hours, and there was no argument that could save them. That part, at least, was settled, and settling it felt almost like relief.

They worked without discussing who had decided what. Emile wrapped the chicken and the burgers in foil and set them by the fire ring for the raccoons, far from the table, and Emilee ferried the melon and tomatoes to the ice. The macaroni he stood over for a long moment. His aunt had made it from scratch and would ask about it tomorrow. He thought about the hours, about the heat, about how the dish had sat in a hot car before it ever reached the table, which shortened the count even further, and he carried it to the foil pile.

"Your aunt's going to be sad," Emilee said.

"My aunt would rather be sad than sick. So would my dad." He was less certain about his mother, who hated waste with a conviction she had inherited rather than chosen, but he found he was willing to be the one who held the line tonight, and also willing to admit he might hear about it at breakfast.

The potato salad had come out of the cooler at one, which put it past the hour but under the two, and the two, he kept reminding himself, belonged to the cooler temperature. Above 90 the rule was stricter. He set it with the foil pile too, then wiped down the table while Emilee latched the cooler and dragged it back into the poplar's shadow.

Down at the lake his father was folding the chairs, unbothered, the evening light making an archipelago of the islands offshore. Emile called out that dinner was handled, that the good stuff was on ice, and his father raised a hand without looking up. Emilee handed him the last dishtowel.

"You're going to check that thermometer again before bed, aren't you," she said.

"I'm going to move the cooler closer to the water first," he said. "It's colder down there."

activity: to debate a current issue entirely in a new language for five minutes
knowledge_domain: to debate a current issue entirely in a new language for five minutes
fact: Linguist Merrill Swain's output hypothesis holds that trying to speak or write a language makes learners notice gaps in what they know, which helps them learn.
story:
Rachel had chosen the hostel in Lyon partly for the free breakfast and partly because Jon and Leon were on the same school language trip, and partly, though she would not have said this out loud, because the trip brochure promised a debate practicum. Her parents were somewhere in the Rhône valley with a rented car and a guidebook; she was in a classroom above a boulangerie with a fan that clicked every fourth rotation, preparing to argue, in French, for five continuous minutes, that the city should close its centre to cars.

She had read eleven articles in French that week. She could recognise every word on the page. On Thursday evening, sitting on the hostel steps with Jon, she tried to say her opening line aloud and stopped after eight words. "Fermer le centre-ville aux voitures," she said, and then nothing came. She had wanted to say that delivery drivers would suffer, and she could not find "suffer." She knew "travail." She knew "voitures." Between them lay a gap shaped exactly like her argument.

"That's the thing, though," Jon said, peeling an orange with his thumb. "Swain's output hypothesis. Trying to speak makes you notice the gaps in what you know, and noticing them is how you learn." He said it like a slogan he had memorised for the midterm. Rachel had skipped that chapter, because she had assumed that input, reading and listening, was everything, and that speaking would simply arrive once enough French had accumulated in her, the way water fills a jug.

So she changed her method. On Friday she stood at the mirror in the shared bathroom and argued at her own reflection, and every time she stalled she wrote the missing word on her wrist with a pen. By Saturday her wrist read: malgré, livreur, prudence, quiconque. The list was humiliating and useful at the same time. When Leon found her rehearsing in the courtyard, gesticulating at a bicycle rack as though it were a hostile audience, he said nothing for a while, because he was reticent by nature, then offered to play the opposition. "You'll need someone to disagree with," he said. "Otherwise it's not a debate, it's a sermon."

They argued for two hours. Leon, whose French was genuinely fluent, took the drivers' side and made it sound reasonable, which annoyed her, because she had wanted him to be wrong. She discovered that she could equivocate in French now, saying "certes" and then pivoting with "cependant," and she noticed that this made her a better debater and a less honest one. At one point she tried to say "I choose the metro" and produced instead a sentence that, according to Leon, announced that she shocked the metro. Jon laughed until he had to sit down on the wall. The whole courtyard laughed, the hostel cat, a man delivering sparkling water, everybody.

The debate itself was held on Monday evening in the classroom above the boulangerie, before an audience of nine: the other students, the instructor, and Mr. Ricci, a retired neighbour from the building who attended every event because he had opinions about traffic and nothing else to do on Mondays. Rachel spoke for five minutes and twelve seconds. Her third sentence wobbled and her conclusion came in a rushed conditional tense she had not known she possessed, but the argument held. She used "malgré." She used "livreur." Mr. Ricci heckled her in a Provençal accent about his parking spot, and she answered him, in French, without planning to.

Afterward the instructor gave her the score sheet and a short comment, and Leon translated the comment even though she could read it: structured, persuasive, some errors, brave. She walked out onto the street carrying the paper, and Jon caught up with her at the corner. "So you convinced me," he said. "Cars should stay out. I came in on your side and you kept me there."

"That's the problem," Rachel said. "I only found out what I think by trying to say it, and now I'm not sure the argument is mine or just the one I had words for." She looked at the score sheet, at the word "persuasive," and then down the narrow street, where a delivery van was double-parked outside the boulangerie, hazards blinking, driver running inside for a baguette. "Give me a topic I've never rehearsed," she said, "and I'll tell you what I believe in about forty seconds, with a lot of hand gestures."

activity: to compute the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates
knowledge_domain: to compute the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates
fact: Two parallel plates 0.02 metres apart with 100 volts across them produce an electric field of 5,000 volts per metre between them.
story:
The kitchen table had been Mathis's since seven o'clock, and by nine it held two sharpened pencils, a cold mug of tea, and a worksheet from Mr. García's class that he had read so many times the words had started to feel like wallpaper. The problem showed two parallel plates, 0.02 metres apart, with 100 volts across them, and asked for the electric field strength at a point between the plates. He had answered fifty volts per metre, and something about the smallness of it had bothered him all evening without his being able to say why.

Shay let himself in through the back door the way he always did, shaking rain off his jacket, carrying his little brother's laptop under one arm like a pizza box. "Is your dad home?"

"Upstairs. Why?"

"Because I need the internet and ours got cut." Shay set the laptop on the table and pushed the worksheet aside to make room. "Don't move that, I'm just looking." He looked anyway, and read for a moment, and then tapped the second line of Mathis's working with one finger. "Where'd the two come from?"

"The separation. It's two centimetres."

"Your other numbers say metres."

Mathis looked at the page. The problem said 0.02 metres, and he had copied it as 2, which was true in centimetres and false in the way the formula cared about. He could feel his ears going warm. "So it's off by..."

"A hundred times too small," Shay said, not unkindly, and then, because he was Shay, "I did the same thing in my exam. Mr. García circled it in red and wrote 'units' like I'd betrayed him personally."

Judith arrived twenty minutes later with her own books, because Tuesdays had become a habit none of them had ever proposed out loud. She was saving for a chemistry tutor her mother couldn't pay for, since her father's business had slid into insolvency over the winter and the family had started speaking about money in a lower voice, as if the word itself might hear them. She sat down, saw Mathis's crossed-out working, and asked what had happened.

"I divided by two instead of nought point nought two," Mathis said. "So I got fifty volts per metre, and the real answer is five thousand." Saying it out loud made it worse and better at once. Five thousand sounded like a real thing, a force you could almost feel, and fifty sounded like nothing, like a number you'd invent to make a sum come out tidy.

Judith pulled the page toward her and checked it against the problem. "So two parallel plates, nought point nought two metres apart, a hundred volts across them, and you get five thousand volts per metre in between."

"That's it. That's the whole thing." He took the page back and copied the corrected answer in pen so it couldn't be undone, and the act of doing that sensitized him to every unit on the sheet, so that he read the remaining problems half as slowly and twice as carefully, checking each number's letters before he trusted its value.

Shay, meanwhile, had opened the laptop on the counter and was following a repair video with the sound low. His brother had dropped it down a flight of stairs, and the family couldn't afford a shop, and Shay had decided, with the private seriousness he kept for practical things, that he would learn to fix it himself before Christmas. He wanted that the way Judith wanted the tutor: not as a wish but as a debt he owed to someone smaller than him.

"You're doing that thing," Judith said to Mathis, watching him recheck a second problem. "The thing where you punish yourself."

"I'm being careful."

"You already found the mistake. Most people wouldn't have." She said it lightly, but he knew she meant it, because Judith had a jaundiced view of easy reassurance and never handed out a compliment she hadn't tested first.

He wanted to believe her, and at the same time he could feel the shape of what he still didn't know: he could divide a hundred by nought point nought two, and he could say volts per metre, and he could not yet picture what the field was doing in the space between the plates, whether it was uniform like a held breath or something stranger. He said so, out loud, because it seemed dishonest not to. "I got the right answer and I don't actually know what it means yet. That's the part that bothers me."

"That's the part that's next," Judith said, and turned back to her own books, and the table went quiet except for the rain and the low murmur of Shay's video, where a man with steady hands was removing a tiny screw from a place a screw had no business being.

Mathis worked the third problem slowly, converting everything to metres first, before he touched the rest of it. Under the counter Shay held up a removed keyboard, grinned at it like it owed him money, and said, "Mathis. Come look at this when you're done."

activity: how social, economic and environmental systems influence one another
knowledge_domain: how social, economic and environmental systems influence one another
fact: The Soviet Union diverted the Amu Darya and Syr Darya rivers to irrigate cotton, and the shrinking, saltier Aral Sea lost a fishing industry that had employed about 40,000 people.
story:
Jasmine had promised the school paper an editorial by Friday, and by Wednesday afternoon she still had only a title: "Give the Valley Its Water." The proposal before the county was simple enough on its surface. Farmers upstream wanted a larger allocation from the river to irrigate a new stretch of alfalfa, and everyone downstream, including her town, would get whatever was left. Her father drove a truck for the cannery and had opinions about farmers. Her editor wanted eight hundred words with a strong stance.

She took the corner table at the library where the outlet actually worked and spread out her notes. Kelvin slid into the chair across from her without asking. "You're writing the water thing," he said. "My uncle's one of the farmers. He says without the allocation he loses the back forty." He set his phone face down on the table, which for Kelvin was a gesture of seriousness.

"So write a rebuttal," Jasmine said. "We can run both."

"I'm not going to change anyone's mind. Nobody changes anyone's mind." He picked up one of her printouts, a county map with the river drawn in blue, and traced the line with his finger from the mountains down through the valley, past the town, past the cannery, off the bottom edge of the page. "Where does it even go after this?"

"Does it matter?"

He shrugged and gave her back the map.

Mr. Dang came by with the returns cart and paused at their table, because Jasmine had six books stacked in a teeter and none of them checked out. "Research for the editorial?" he asked. "If you want examples of water disputes, the environmental science section has case studies. Big ones." He wrote a call number on a slip of scrap paper and moved on, and Jasmine took the slip mostly out of politeness, and then, because the article was due and she had nothing, she went and found the shelf.

The book she opened had a photograph of ships sitting on cracked ground, tilted, far from any water. She read the caption twice. Kelvin appeared behind her with his own book about dams and read over her shoulder. "That can't be right," he said. "A sea drying up."

"It's right," she said, and copied the sentence into her notebook word for word: the Soviet Union had diverted the Amu Darya and the Syr Darya rivers to irrigate cotton, and the shrinking, saltier Aral Sea lost a fishing industry that had employed about 40,000 people. She looked at the number for a while. Forty thousand people, on the far side of the world, in a country that no longer existed, and the cause had been growing cotton.

"That's just the USSR," Kelvin said. "They did things like that. That's not us."

"It's water," Jasmine said. "The water doesn't know what country it's in."

He didn't answer, and she went back to the table and sat with the fact. She tried to introspect, honestly, about why the sentence bothered her so much, and what she found was not sympathy for distant fishermen but something more uncomfortable: her editorial was not really about water at all. It was about whose job mattered, her father's or Kelvin's uncle's, and she had picked her father's without ever asking what happened to the third people downstream, the ones with no name in the argument at all.

That evening Elsie texted her a photo of a petition, signed already by half the soccer team. Everyone she knew was signing it. She typed back that she was still thinking, and Elsie replied with three question marks, and Jasmine set the phone on her desk and didn't look at it again.

She drafted the editorial twice and threw both away. On Thursday she wrote something else instead, a letter to the paper's editor, which was Elsie, and left it in her locker between classes. In it she laid out the Aral Sea plainly, without the editorial's certainty, and then she did the harder thing and admitted what she didn't know. She did not know how much water the alfalfa would actually take, or whether the river here was anything like those rivers, or whether the people downstream of her town even existed in any organized way to object. What she proposed was small and specific: that the county publish, before the vote, an account of what flowed out the far end of the valley now, so that whatever it became later could be measured against something. She signed it and felt the strange clemency of having written to a friend instead of at her enemies, because for once the letter asked for information rather than for someone's defeat.

Friday the piece ran, letters page, under her name. She stood near the library doors reading it while people walked past. A woman from the cannery, disaffected and loud at every council meeting, was outside on the steps telling anyone who would listen that the paper had gone soft. Kelvin came out and stood next to Jasmine without looking at her.

"My uncle called it communist propaganda," he said. "Then he read it again."

"Is that good or bad?"

"He wants to know who's downstream of us. He says nobody's ever asked him that." Kelvin held up his phone, showing a message he'd started to the county water office, the cursor blinking in the empty field after "To whom it may concern." He looked at Jasmine. "What do I even put here?"

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: French engineer Maximilien Ringelmann, publishing in 1913, found that people pulling a rope in a group each pulled less hard than they did alone.
story:
The pool at the far end of the sports complex was drained for repairs, so the water polo team trained in the diving well, a square of green water that smelled of chlorine and old rope. Joseph had joined in September because Patrick said it would look good on applications, and had stayed because, somewhere in October, he had begun to love the game itself, the held breath, the violence under the surface that nobody in the stands could see. Now it was February, regionals in three weeks, and the coach had them doing rope work: towing a weighted sled across the shallow end while the whole team pushed from behind, hands on the tow line, legs churning.

"Again," the coach called. "That was embarrassing."

Joseph's shoulders burned. They ran the drill six more times, and each time the sled crawled, and each time the coach swore at them with something close to affection. Afterward, toweling off in the tiled corridor, Gibson sat down beside him and pulled up something on his phone. "You know there's a name for this," Gibson said. "This French engineer, Maximilien Ringelmann, publishing in 1913. He found that people pulling a rope in a group each pulled less hard than they did alone."

"Sounds like an excuse," Joseph said.

"Sounds like physics," Gibson said, and went to find his goggles.

The fact mesmerized Joseph all the same. He thought about it during his turn in the lifeguard chair on Saturdays, watching the lap swimmers, and he thought about it Monday when the coach split them for time trials. Each boy towed the sled alone, individually timed, and Joseph beat his own expectation by four seconds. Patrick, who coasted during team drills, went even harder alone, beating everyone. "You sandbag us every Tuesday," Joseph told him in the changing room. "Me?" Patrick said, wringing out his suit. "You were watching me?" Joseph hadn't been, exactly, but he let it stand.

That week Joseph began counting strokes instead of effort. It was a small dishonesty, he admitted to himself, a way of not asking whether he was one of the people the French engineer had measured. At practice on Thursday he pushed until his arms shook, and the sled still crawled, and he understood that his shaking arms made no difference that anyone could see. That was the part nobody said out loud. The team was a machine for hiding effort, and also, on the two fast breaks they ran that night, a machine for making something none of them could make alone: Patrick's blind pass arriving at his hand a half second before the defender, as if the water had carried it there on its own.

Ms. Menon taught his statistics class, and on Friday he stayed after to ask her about the study. She rummaged in a drawer for a photocopy and handed it over without ceremony. "Design like that gets argued about," she said. "But it's been replicated plenty. Groups pull less per person. Whether that's laziness or something else, the data doesn't say." He liked that she didn't tidy it up for him. His father would have called the whole thing a bromide about teamwork going soft, and his mother would have said the opposite, that the group makes us better than we are, and both of them would have been partly right, which was the problem with things people said about groups.

At the last hard practice before regionals, Joseph asked the coach if they could run the sled drill alone, each of them, one at a time, while the others watched. "You want to be timed in front of the team," the coach said. "Everyone does." The coach blew the whistle. Gibson went first and was visibly faster alone, and so was Joseph, and so was a sophomore nobody expected anything from, a quiet kid who pulled like the rope owed him money. The team stood in the shallows and watched each other be strong, and something in the air changed, though Joseph couldn't have said what, exactly, and didn't trust anyone who claimed they could.

They lost at regionals by two goals in overtime. It was not a story where watching each other pull alone fixed everything; the other team had a left-handed hole set they never solved, and Patrick missed a five-meter shot that hit the crossbar so hard the sound carried into the parking lot. Afterward, in the corridor outside the changing rooms, the team stood around not wanting to leave, and Gibson put his wet hand on Joseph's neck and left it there.

"Same time next season," Patrick said. "Sled and everything."

Joseph nodded. He still didn't know whether the group had made them try less, or whether trying alone was just easier to see, easier to be proud of, and he suspected he would go on not knowing. His suit was still dripping into his shoes. "Towels first," he said, and pushed open the door to the changing room.

activity: to write a historiographical essay on how views of the French Revolution have changed since 1800
knowledge_domain: to write a historiographical essay on how views of the French Revolution have changed since 1800
fact: Socialist politician Jean Jaurès wrote a socialist history of the French Revolution in the early 1900s that shaped the class-conflict interpretation dominant for much of the twentieth century.
story:
Layla spread the books across the kitchen table after dinner, while the dishwasher hissed and her mother dried a saucepan a few feet away. The assignment sheet lay at the top, weighted down with a mug: a historiographical essay on how interpretations of the French Revolution had changed since 1800. She had expected the Revolution itself to be the difficulty, the Terror, the guillotine, the crowds, but the teacher wanted no crowds at all. He wanted what historians had said about the crowds, and why they had said it, and how one version had displaced another.

The problem was that she could not find the hinge. The early accounts in her stack treated the Revolution as a moral drama or a cautionary tale, then something shifted, and by the middle of the twentieth century everyone was writing about class. The books said so in passing, in prefaces, in footnotes she had to chase through three volumes at once, and the cause of the shift stayed out of reach, like a word she kept almost remembering.

Reese arrived at nine with a bag of clementines and no interest in the French Revolution. He was applying to film school and wanted an audience for his portfolio edit, and he had decided Layla, who owed him for driving her to the library twice, was the audience. He set his laptop on the counter and opened it. Two minutes, he said, and then I'll leave you to your funeral.

She watched. The short film was mostly rain on windows, shot in a melancholic green light, with a boy running nowhere in particular. It was good in places, and she said so, and Reese exhaled like a man released. He ate a clementine while she went back to the table, and he read over her shoulder because he could not help reading over shoulders.

"Who's Jaurès?" he asked. He was pointing at a note she had written to herself after finding the name buried in an introduction, spelled with an accent she had copied carefully.

"A politician," she said. "French. Socialist. But look." She turned the book so he could see. In the early 1900s he had written a whole history of the Revolution, and it was a socialist history, a history told from that conviction. And it had not stayed one book among many. The interpretation it carried, the Revolution as class conflict, became the dominant one for much of the twentieth century. A politician had walked into the archive and rerouted it.

"So a guy who wanted to emancipate workers also wrote the book everyone believed about 1789," Reese said, peeling another clementine. He seemed pleased with himself, and Layla found she was pleased too, because his blunt version had clarified something for her. She had been hunting for a neutral cause of the shift, some slow accumulation of evidence, and instead there was a person, with commitments, writing from inside them.

She wrote for another hour while Reese dozed on the couch and her mother went up to bed. She drafted a paragraph setting the socialist account against the earlier moral drama as a counterpoint, then stopped herself, because counterpoint implied equal weight, and that was not what she meant. The weight had moved. What she could not settle was whether Jaurès's politics had made him see something true or only something useful, and every time she tried to phrase the question neutrally it came out slanted. She left the question in the draft, open, and underlined it as a thing she did not know, which felt like both honesty and defeat.

Reese woke when she closed her laptop. He asked, gathering his coat, whether the essay would get her into a good college, and she said probably not, it was just homework, and he looked genuinely disappointed, because he had decided somewhere in the evening that her work mattered in a way his rain footage did not. She told him the footage mattered, and meant it, and watched him not believe her.

At the door he paused. "So your guy," he said. "The socialist one. Did he win, in the end? Did his version beat the others?"

"It held the field for most of a century," Layla said. "Then people started arguing back."

"Good," Reese said, shouldering his bag. "Then there's hope for me too." He went down the front steps two at a time, and through the window she saw him stop at the gate, take out his phone, and start filming the empty street.

activity: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
knowledge_domain: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
fact: A preprint is a paper posted publicly before peer review, so its findings have not yet been checked by independent experts chosen by a journal.
story:
Kaylee printed both articles at the library because she could not think well in tabs, and now they lay side by side on the kitchen table like two witnesses who disagreed about the same car crash. The question they both claimed to answer was whether social media use changed adolescent sleep, and the first article, forty pages of tidy regression tables from a journal with a long name, said the effect was small, almost nothing. The second said the opposite, loudly, with graphs that looked like a mountain range. She needed twelve hundred words by Friday that did not just summarize each one in turn, that compared them, and she had promised Mr. Kerr, who had agreed to read a draft even though the assignment belonged to her first-year seminar, that she would have something for him by Thursday night.

The house was empty until six, which was the only good thing about her mother's new shift. Kaylee read with a pen, wrote "better sample" in the margin of the first article and "bold" in the margin of the second, and then stopped, because she realized she had no idea how to weigh boldness against a better sample. She ate three crackers without tasting them. When she flipped to the last page of the second article to find the journal's name, there was no journal. There was only a banner across the top of the PDF, grey and quiet, that said "Preprint" and then a sentence underneath it, small as a nutrition label.

She read it twice. Posted publicly before peer review. Findings not yet checked by independent experts chosen by a journal. So the mountain-range graphs had gone out into the world without anyone chosen by a journal sitting down to test them first. She sat back, and the chair creaked, and she felt something between cheated and relieved, because for two days she had treated the two articles as equals and now she could not.

She texted Skylar: "is my whole paper dead." Skylar called back from the break room at the garden center, where Kaylee could hear the hiss of the hose and someone saying the word invoice repeatedly. "Dead how," Skylar said. "Which article is the problem." "The loud one. It's a preprint." "Which means what, in English." "It was posted publicly before peer review. Nobody independent, chosen by a journal, has checked it yet." There was a pause with water in it. "So it's basically a rumor with graphs." "That's harsh." "That's your paper, though. You get to say why the checked one deserves more weight and whether the unchecked one still earns any."

That was the hinge, and Kaylee knew it, and it was not comfortable. Because the preprint was not stupid. Its sample was enormous, drawn from three countries, while the journal article followed one parochial cohort of students from a single county, as if that county were the whole world. The preprint's methods section underpinned its dramatic claims more carefully than she had first credited, and when she re-read it she found herself admiring the way it confessed its own limits, which was more than the published article did. She spread both articles out and put a mug on each one, the blue mug on the checked article and the chipped one on the preprint, like assigning them to opposite corners of a very small ring.

Andre arrived at seven with his calculus book and the specific hunger of someone who knows where the crackers are. He read the grey banner while chewing. "So they just put it out there," he said. "Before anyone checks it." "That's what a preprint is. Posted publicly, before peer review, no independent experts chosen by a journal have looked yet." "Sounds like something my uncle does with football opinions." "Your uncle doesn't run regressions." "His confidence-to-evidence ratio is worse, I'll give you that." He stole a fourth cracker and went to the couch, and Kaylee stayed at the table, because something was finally moving.

She opened a blank document and typed the sentence she had been avoiding: the two articles disagreed, and part of learning to review them was learning what each one was. The journal article carried the weight of review, which was not the same as carrying the weight of truth; reviewers could be wrong, and journals could be slow, and the preprint's authors had decided speed mattered more than the waiting. What she could not do, she wrote, was pretend the two were equally certain. The checked one earned more trust; the unchecked one earned more attention. Then she deleted that, because it sounded like a mug slogan, and wrote instead that the honest position was to hold the published finding as the sturdier floor while letting the preprint define the size of the room, and even as she typed it she could hear how provisional it was, how much it admitted it did not know.

At six her mother came home smelling of the hospital cafeteria and asked, from the doorway, whether Kaylee had eaten anything with a vegetable in it, and Kaylee said there were tomatoes in the crackers, probably, and her mother made the sound of a person who has given up on that argument but not on the war. Mr. Kerr emailed at eight: send whatever you have, messy is fine. She sent him nine hundred words with a paragraph in the middle that said, plainly, that she could not yet say how much the preprint's findings should be discounted, only that discounting them entirely and ignoring them entirely were both ways of not thinking.

Afterward she sat with both articles still pinned under their mugs, and Andre looked up from his derivatives and said, "So which one's right?" She pulled the blue mug toward herself and drank the cold dregs of the tea she had forgotten to make, and said, "Ask me in twelve hundred words."

activity: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
knowledge_domain: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
fact: The InVID-WeVerify browser plugin, built by a European Union-funded project, splits a video into key frames that can be reverse-searched.
story:
The video arrived in the group chat at 7:14 in the morning, and by 7:20 Sara had already typed a caption in all capitals: THIS IS HAPPENING AT THE RIVER. It showed a bridge buckling, water the color of milk chocolate, a man's voice repeating something in a language she couldn't place. Forty people were in the chat. She pressed send before her toast was done.

By second period, Madisyn had reposted it with three exclamation points, and someone Sara didn't know had added a claim that two students from the neighboring district had been on that bridge. Mr. Le stopped his physiology lecture midway through a diagram of the heart, looked at the twenty phones glowing under desks, and said, "Whatever that is, it can wait twelve minutes." His tone was laconic, almost bored, which somehow made everyone put their phones away faster than anger would have. Sara slid hers under her binder, but the shape of the video stayed with her, the way the bridge folded inward like paper.

At lunch, Imran was the only one at the table not talking about it. "You didn't see it?" Sara asked. He said he had, at his mom's office yesterday, a week before anyone posted it to the chat. Sara frowned. "Then why didn't you say anything?" He shrugged and pulled out his laptop. "A guy at her work, they do fact-checking. He showed me a plugin. It's called InVID-WeVerify." He typed while he talked. "The InVID-WeVerify browser plugin, built by a European Union-funded project, splits a video into key frames that can be reverse-searched." He turned the screen so she could see. "You drop the link in here."

She watched the plugin chop the video into still frames, a row of thumbnails like film negatives laid out on a lightbox. "You can search each one," Imran said. "Like a reverse image search, but for the frames." Madisyn leaned over Sara's shoulder, arms crossed, still defending the post. "It's from the river," she said. "Someone said the water tower's in the background."

Sara dragged the sharpest frame into the search bar. The results loaded slowly, the cafeteria wifi hiccupping, and she held her breath without deciding to. The oldest match was dated four years ago, a news article from a different country entirely, the same buckling bridge above a caption about seasonal flooding. Not their river. Not this week. Not two students from the neighboring district, who probably did not exist.

Madisyn went quiet, then said, "I told my little sister not to go near the water today." She said it flatly, but Sara heard what was underneath it: the small dread she had passed along to someone who trusted her. "Okay," Madisyn said. "So I repost something saying it's old." Sara hesitated. That was the instinct, to correct loudly, the same urgency that had made her send it at 7:20. But a correction could also travel without its proof and turn into a second rumor, the claim that the video was fake, floating free of the four-year-old article the way the original had floated free of its date. "Maybe we just tell the people who asked us directly," Sara said. "And show them how we checked." Imran nodded. "The guy at my mom's office says the correction rarely catches up."

She spent study hall drafting a message to the chat, deleting versions that sounded either defensive or smug. It was strange to sit with both things at once: the video was old, that much was certain, and still she could not be certain where it had first come from, or why someone had re-dated it, or whether the man's frightened voice on the soundtrack belonged to that bridge at all. She had wanted the sharing to be simple, a kindness even, a warning. It had been a warning about nothing, aimed at people she liked, and she could not decide whether that made it harmless or worse than a lie someone had chosen on purpose. She didn't pathologize the impulse to share, though. Mr. Le, passing behind her, had said something earlier that stuck: wanting to protect people wasn't a disease, it just needed the brakes checked. She wasn't sure the brakes were what she'd installed today, or only a better mirror.

She sent the short version at 3:40: the video is from four years ago, here's the article, here's the plugin if you want to check things yourself. Then she closed the laptop, found Madisyn at her locker, and said, "Text your sister. Tell her the river's fine."

activity: getting a first part-time job
knowledge_domain: getting a first part-time job
fact: Montana is the one US state where, after a probationary period, an employer generally needs good cause to fire a worker, under its 1987 Wrongful Discharge from Employment Act.
story:
Ryder counted the money in his wallet twice on the bus, as if the second count might change the first. Eleven dollars and some change, and the prom fees and the deposit for the dorm orientation still unpaid, which was why he was riding toward Halstead's Grocery with a folded application sweating in his back pocket. Cristian had texted him that morning: just act like you already work there, nobody can tell the difference. Ryder did not believe this, but he read it three times anyway.

The manager, a heavy man named Mr. Weeks who kept a pen behind each ear, looked at the application for less time than Ryder had spent filling it out. "Saturdays and two evenings," he said. "Ninety days probation. After that you're regular." He held out a shirt with the store logo already faded at the shoulder. Ryder took it before he had decided to.

That night he called Cristian, who was in Billings for the month with his father. "Probation," Cristian said, before Ryder could describe the shirt. "You know Montana's the only state where, after probation, a boss generally has to have good cause to fire you? It's called the Wrongful Discharge from Employment Act, 1987." Ryder said he did not know that, and Cristian said his cousin in Texas had spent an hour arguing the opposite, that a boss could cut you for any reason at all, even a bad mood, and Cristian had finally looked it up on his phone just to end the argument. "So enjoy that," Cristian said, "whereas the rest of us live like it's the Wild West."

The following Saturday Ryder reported to the produce section, where Ms. Flores, who had retired from teaching the year before and now stacked lettuce four mornings a week, showed him how to rotate the older containers to the front. She moved with a speed that seemed to contradict her age. "They pay me a little honorarium, if you can call it that, to come talk at the college's career day each spring," she said, repositioning a wilted head of romaine. "A flat thank-you sum. Not a wage. I tell them it's the only job I've ever had where being underpaid is built into the word." Ryder laughed, and she watched him struggle with the pricing gun until he got it right, and then she did not watch him anymore, which he understood as a kind of respect.

The work enervated him by the third hour, not because it was heavy but because it was unbroken, the same reaching and lifting and turning, and he found himself inventing small systems to make the time feel like his own. He grouped the peppers by shade. He learned which customers wanted bags and which waved them off. Sidney came through on her break from the bakery and leaned on his cart and said, "So you're the putative produce expert now," and when he looked uncertain she said, "Supposed. Supposed expert. You've been here one Saturday." He threw a lime at her, softly, and she caught it.

In the second week Mr. Weeks stopped him by the registers. "You rotated those apples wrong," he said. "Cost us a crate." Ryder felt his face go hot, and he also felt, underneath the heat, a strange steadiness, the thought that he was still inside ninety days and could be cut loose tomorrow for less than this, and that after ninety days it would take something more, something with cause behind it, at least here, at least in this state, and that this fact did not protect him from being wrong, only from being discarded. He said, "Show me which way is right and I'll do it that way." Mr. Weeks looked at him for a moment, then walked him back to produce and demonstrated the rotation without speaking, twice, slowly.

That night he called Cristian again. "So the Montana thing," Ryder said. "It's not like a shield. Weeks can still make my life miserable, he just can't cut me loose for nothing, after probation." Cristian said, "Which is more than my cousin's got," and in the background his cousin's voice rose, disputing something, and Cristian said he had to go defend the facts of history.

Ryder hung up and took the faded shirt off its hook, and it looked different to him now, less like a costume and more like a thing he was going to have to wash and fold and keep. He had not decided yet whether he would stay past the summer. He only knew that on Monday he would stack the apples the correct way, and that Ms. Flores would notice, and would say nothing, and that this was the kind of small victory he was currently willing to accept. He set his alarm for six, put the shirt in the hamper, and turned off the light.

activity: to compute the integral of a function to find the area under a curve
knowledge_domain: to compute the integral of a function to find the area under a curve
fact: The area under the curve y equals x squared, from x equals 0 to x equals 1, is exactly one third.
story:
The last week of August belonged to her grandmother's kitchen table, which smelled of lavender and pencil shavings, and Maelle had promised herself she would pass the placement exam on Monday even if it meant giving up the lake with everyone else. She had failed the diagnostic in June by four points. Four points, and the advisor had suggested she might want to "consider her options," a phrase Maelle wanted to litigate on the spot, to argue down to its bones, except arguing with the advisor would not change the number on the page. Only the number on the page mattered. So she was here, at the table by the window, with a roll of graph paper her grandmother kept for drawing quilt patterns.

The exam would have one question she could already name: find the area under a curve. She understood, in a vague way, that the integral was the tool for this, that it existed, that somewhere in the textbook it waited for her with its long S shape. But she did not trust tools she could not see working. So on the first evening she drew the curve herself, y equals x squared, on the graph paper, from x equals zero to x equals one, a parabola that started flat and climbed steeply toward the corner of the square. Then she started counting boxes.

Counting was its own kind of honesty. A box cut by the curve was only partly inside, so she halved some, eyeballed others, argued with herself the way her mother argued with the insurance people on the phone, estimating and conceding and estimating again. Half a box under the left side, more than half near the top where the curve stood almost vertical. When she totaled it all, shading as she went, she got a little over one third of the whole square. A third of one, roughly. She sat back and looked at it. The answer felt smaller than the effort deserved, and she did not know yet whether that meant she'd counted wrong or whether smallness was just the truth of the thing.

She texted Kiersten a photo of the shaded paper. Kiersten replied from the lake, a picture of Reed midair off the dock, then: "why are you doing math with paper like a pilgrim." Then, a minute later, "did you learn the actual integral yet or are you just coloring." Maelle typed and deleted three replies. Kiersten meant well; Kiersten always meant well. But there was something in the question that stung, the suggestion that the counting was quaint, extrinsic to the real work, a decoration rather than the work itself, and Maelle did not fully believe that. She believed it a little, which was worse.

On Saturday her grandmother watched her from the stove, stirring something, saying nothing, which was her way of staying close without intruding. Maelle worked through the textbook section slowly. The notation looked like a gate she didn't have the key to. What finally opened it was not the textbook but the graph paper itself: she cut the shaded region out with her grandmother's fabric scissors, weighed it on the kitchen scale against the full square she'd cut and weighed first. The shaded piece came out to almost exactly a third of the full square's weight. Two separate methods, the counting and the scale, agreeing. The area under the curve from zero to one was one third. She said it out loud to the kitchen, and her grandmother said, "That's nice, dear," without turning around, and something in the plainness of that made Maelle laugh for the first time in days.

The integral itself she cracked on Sunday morning, at the same table, with the window open. When the formula gave her one third, the same one third, exactly, she felt the specific vertigo of two worlds clicking together: the shaded scraps on the table and the abstract machinery in the book, both pointing at the same truth, one by sweat and approximation, one by clean steps that arrived without sweating at all. She understood now why her teacher, Mr. Liu, kept saying the exam wanted reasoning, not memorization. She wished she had listened to him in June instead of defending her study habits like a lawyer defending a client she privately doubted.

She missed the lake. That was the cost, and she was honest with herself about it: Kiersten had sent one more photo, the whole group on the dock at sunset, and Maelle had looked at it for a long time before putting the phone face down. Reed had written "come tomorrow, the water's perfect" and she had written back "Monday I test" and nothing after that, and the nothing sat in her chest like a swallowed stone. You could have the area under the curve or you could have the last weekend of summer with people you might not see the same way after September, and it occurred to her that nobody had ever told her the two things were measured on the same paper, that the trade was even real until you made it.

Sunday evening she redrew the parabola from memory, no textbook, no graph paper, just the curve and the interval zero to one, and did it again, and got one third again. Her grandmother came to the table with two cups of tea and set one down beside the paper.

"Tell me what it says," her grandmother said, pulling out the other chair.

"It says the space under the curve is exactly a third. I checked it three ways."

Her grandmother picked up the drawing and held it to the window, against the last of the light.

activity: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
knowledge_domain: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
fact: In Chicago, MLA and APA styles, entries in the final list of sources are arranged alphabetically by the author's surname, not in the order the sources were cited.
story:
I had the whole thing under control, which is what I kept telling myself while the kitchen table disappeared under books I had not opened. My mother had left coffee at my elbow at ten and taken it away cold at midnight, and in between I had produced four pages, eight footnotes, and a thesis so sharp I could have cut bread with it: that the hedonistic culture of the 1920s press was not the cause of Prohibition's failure, only its most convenient excuse. I remember feeling very good about those four pages. I remember that specifically because it turned out to be the last time in the whole night I felt good about anything.

Arianna came over at eleven because I texted her "bibliography emergency," which, in fairness, I had also texted her twice before about things that were not emergencies. She smelled like the outside, cold air and bus diesel, and she pulled off her gloves finger by finger while she read. Her fingertips were still pink from the walk when she flattened my works cited page against the table, next to the sugar bowl and a ring my coffee cup had left on the wood.

"Your footnotes go Evans, then Okafor, then Marino," she said. "Your bibliography goes Evans, Marino, Okafor." I told her that was how I'd used them, chronologically, which made sense, because I had found Evans first. She tapped the page twice, the way she tapped a fence rail before vaulting it in gym class. "In Chicago, MLA and APA, entries in the final list of sources are arranged alphabetically by the author's surname, not in the order the sources were cited." She said it flat, like reading a bus schedule, and waited.

I said that seemed backwards. She said it didn't matter what it seemed, that was how it was, and that if I reordered the citations too, the whole apparatus would sing. So we did that, or she did it and I watched, her pen moving down the margins of my printout, and my chest did that thing where it palpitated once, hard, the way it does before a race starts, and I told myself it was excitement about the paper. It might have been. I am still not the person to ask.

Here is the part I left out when I told people this story afterward: the four pages were not exactly mine. My brother had written a paper on Prohibition two years ago for the same class, same teacher, Ms. Campbell-Brown, and his laptop was still in the house because he had left it when he moved out in September, left it and the desk lamp and a note about restitution for the phone bill he'd never paid. I had read his paper once, twice, and then my own draft started sounding like it. Not copied. Echoed. I kept saying "echoed" to myself the way you keep smoothing a crease in paper that keeps coming back.

Arianna turned a page and stopped. "Who's Delgado?" she asked. "You don't cite Delgado anywhere in the text." I looked at the entry, third in the alphabet now, and my face went hot enough that I could feel the kitchen's cold window behind me by contrast. Delgado was in my brother's paper. He had cited Delgado in a footnote I had cut, and I must have copied his bibliography wholesale and then pruned the body, and the alphabet had kept the ghost. Arianna didn't say anything for a moment. The radiator ticked. Somewhere under the table my sock had found a piece of dried rice from dinner and I pressed it flat under my toe, over and over.

"You wrote this," she said, and it was not a question, so it did not require the truth, but I gave it anyway, or part of it, the part about the echo, and watched her face do arithmetic I could not see the sum of.
