She pushed the pages back across the table toward me, all of them, and the last page slid off the edge and landed face down on the floor, the alphabetical list pressed against the tile.

"Rewrite it," she said, standing, pulling her gloves back on. "You have till Thursday. Start with Delgado, actually read Delgado, and see if you even agree with him." She put her hand on the doorframe and paused, and I thought she was going to say something forgiving, something that would let me keep the four pages. "And alphabetize it yourself this time," she said. "It's not hard. You just have to have actually used the sources."

I sat back down after the door shut. I picked the page up off the tile, smoothed it against my knee, and turned it over, and there was Delgado, sitting quietly between the names I knew and the names I didn't, in his proper alphabetical place, waiting to be earned.

activity: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
knowledge_domain: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
fact: Frida Kahlo's The Two Fridas (1939) is a large, nearly square oil painting, about 173 centimetres on each side, showing two seated self-portraits side by side.
story:
The art module at Camp Wren Lake met in the boathouse, where the smell of varnish and lake water did battle with the smell of poster paint. Mr. Halvorsen had pinned a reproduction of The Two Fridas to the plywood wall and told them their critique was due Friday, spoken aloud, five minutes, no reading off the page. Alex had spent the first session saying things like "the colours are sad," which Mr. Halvorsen received with the particular silence of a man collecting evidence.

Wednesday afternoon, with the lake roaring under wind, Alex and Sukhman and Marika commandeered the rec hall, moving the ping-pong table against the wall so they could see the reproduction from farther back. It was small, barely bigger than a hardcover book, and at that size the two women in it looked like a stamp, two figures pressed together in white, one holding scissors and one holding a locket, hearts exposed on both of their dresses.

"You can't talk about composition from here," Sukhman said, chin on his folded arms. "It's a postcard."

"It's not a postcard," Marika said. "It's an art print, and it cost the camp actual money." But she was already digging in the craft cupboard, and she came back with a tape measure and a sheet of paper.

They measured the print together, Marika holding one end flat against the frame while Alex read the number. Twenty-one and a half centimetres wide, twenty-one high. Almost square, but not quite, and that bothered him until Marika, who had looked it up on her phone before the counsellors confiscated signal for the afternoon, said, "The real one is huge. Like a hundred and seventy-three centimetres on each side. Bigger than I am."

"Square?" Alex asked.

"Nearly. And they're both her. Two of the same person, sitting side by side."

He did the arithmetic twice on the paper, dividing, because he wanted to know what standing in front of the actual canvas would feel like. Roughly eight times bigger in each direction. He paced off the rec hall floor, taped a square of masking tape at each corner, eight print-widths by eight print-widths, and then he stood inside it and held the small reproduction at arm's length so its edges lined up with the tape.

"There," he said. "Now it fills the same part of what I see."

The square was bigger than he expected. The two seated figures, if he imagined them blown up to match, would be nearly his own size, and they would not be side by side in a small polite way but filling the whole space, so that a viewer standing close would have to choose one to face. The Frida with the scissors had a cut vein, a heart that leaked onto her skirt; the Frida in Tehuana dress held a small portrait locket, connected by a thin thread of red to the other heart. Sukhman crouched at one taped corner and said the two dresses made a shape like open wings, or like an hourglass if you looked at the sky between them, and that the sky was storm-coloured at the edges and lighter in the middle, right behind the joined hearts.

On Friday the boathouse smelled of rain coming. Alex stood in front of the class with his hands out of his pockets on the second try, and he told them about the square first, how the near-square canvas made him think of a mirror, but a mirror showing the same person twice and torn open. He talked about the diagonal of the blood, the way the white dresses made the red thread the brightest thing in the picture, how the storm sky framed both hearts like a stage. Then he said the part he had argued about with himself all Thursday night.

"The formal stuff is what I can prove," he said. "Composition, colour, the symbolism of the thread and the scissors. But I keep wondering about the size. It's not just big so you'll notice it. It's big so the two of them are the same size as you, standing there. And I don't know which one I'm supposed to be, or if I'm the thing they're both looking at." He paused, hearing how it sounded, and did not take it back. "I can't decide if that's part of the analysis or just something that happened to me."

Mr. Halvorsen wrote something on his clipboard. Marika was nodding slowly, and Sukhman was looking at the print as if he had never seen the scissors before.

"One more thing," Mr. Halvorsen said. "The question you can't decide. Keep it."

After the session Alex walked out to the dock while the first raindrops hit the lake, each one a small flat circle, thousands opening and closing across the grey surface, and he stood there holding his notes until the wind took the top page and carried it out over the water.

activity: professional tone, structured writing and respectful disagreement in formal communication
knowledge_domain: professional tone, structured writing and respectful disagreement in formal communication
fact: Recipients in an email's Bcc field are hidden from everyone else, which is why messages to a long list of people who don't know each other often use Bcc to protect their addresses.
story:
On his third morning at the community center, Maxime was given the key to the supply cupboard and the password to the shared email account, and he understood that these were the same thing in different languages: trust, handed over in small metal and small characters. Ms. Kaya, the volunteer coordinator, spent most of her time on the phone in a voice he had never heard from any adult outside of work, level and unhurried, as if every sentence had been drafted once already. He wanted to learn that voice. He had not yet worked out whether it was something you practiced or something that practice smoothed away.

The trouble surfaced on Thursday. Fifty parents had signed their children up for the summer rowing program, and the schedule had changed, and Ms. Kaya stood at her desk with her reading glasses pushed up into her hair, pasting addresses into an email one at a time. She pasted slowly, and Maxime, sorting life vests in the corner of the office, watched the recipient field stretch longer and longer, name after name accumulating in a single bright line. Something about it bothered him, though at first he could not have said what. Was it that the addresses were parents who did not know each other? He turned the feeling over the way you turn a stone in your pocket, and finally asked.

"Does everyone see all of those, when it sends?"

"That's how email works, isn't it?" Ms. Kaya squinted at the screen. "If I put them in the To line, yes."

He had a half memory of his mother forwarding a newsletter once, and how the top of it had been a column of other people's addresses, dozens of them, like a list of everyone else's houses on a street you'd never walked down. He scrolled his own phone, found the forwarding options in his mail app, and there they were, three fields he had never properly looked at: To, Cc, and a third one. "Bcc," he said aloud. "Recipients in the Bcc field are hidden from everyone else." He said it slowly, testing it. "That's why the newsletter did it, isn't it? For people who don't know each other." Ms. Kaya came around the desk and read over his shoulder, and after a moment she cut the whole line of addresses and pasted it into the hidden field instead.

Vienna, the other intern, arrived at lunch with sandwiches and a blasé shrug about the whole thing, which Maxime had learned was less indifference than a kind of armor. "Everyone's address is already out there somewhere," she said, unwrapping hers. But Sahana, who had been copying the sign-in sheets into a spreadsheet, disagreed, and did it in a way that made Maxime lean in. "It's not about whether it's findable," she said. "It's about whether we're the ones handing it around. Fifty parents, and we'd be publishing them to forty-nine strangers each." She spoke quietly, without heat, and Ms. Kaya actually put down her sandwich to listen.

Maxime realized he was watching a second skill being demonstrated, different from the phone voice but related to it, the way rowing relates to swimming. Sahana disagreed with Vienna and somehow left both of them intact. Vienna argued back, something about consent forms and phone trees, and Sahana said, "That's fair, but those have a purpose the parents chose." Nobody won. Nobody seemed to need to. Maxime kept waiting for the moment when the argument would tip into the kind of disagreement he knew from school, the kind that existed to be won, and it never came.

After lunch Ms. Kaya asked him to draft the email itself, the schedule change, and he sat in front of a blank message for a long time before typing anything. His instinct was to externalize everything, to pour his whole self into it, some joke about the weather, an apology, three exclamation points. But he was beginning to suspect that the professional voice Ms. Kaya used was not a contrivance layered over a person but a kind of architecture, the way a bridge's shape isn't hiding the river, it's how you cross it. He wrote the facts in an order that a stranger could follow, the change first, then the dates, then what to do if it caused a problem, and cut every sentence that existed only to make him feel better about delivering inconvenient news.

He showed Ms. Kaya the draft, and she changed two things: moved a sentence up, softened "must" to "we're asking families to." "Why that one?" he asked, genuinely curious, because to him the original had been clearer. "Because they can't reply to all without writing to me," she said, tapping the screen, where the Bcc field sat, quietly doing its work, holding fifty addresses that none of them would see. "The message goes one way. So the tone has to carry the respect the reply would have carried." He copied that into his notes app under a heading he was slightly embarrassed by, things work is teaching me.

At four o'clock the parents began replying, one at a time, arriving only in the inbox, addressed only to the center. Sahana read a few over his shoulder. "Look at that," she said. "Nobody hit reply all. Nobody could." Vienna, packing her bag, conceded with a grin that this was, in fact, elegant, and asked Maxime whether he thought the whole internet had been built by people making small considerate decisions or by people fixing disasters after the fact. He said he honestly didn't know, that he suspected both, and that he liked not knowing, which made her laugh for some reason.

He locked the supply cupboard and walked out through the gym, where the evening light came in high and flat across the floor, and found himself already drafting, in his head, the message he would send to his mother about the day. He caught himself choosing the tone. Then he just walked home and told her out loud instead, starting with the long bright line of addresses and the hidden field waiting underneath it.

activity: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
knowledge_domain: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
fact: Peter Mitchell proposed in 1961 that cells make ATP using a proton gradient across a membrane, called chemiosmosis, and won the 1978 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
story:
Hudson had failed the cellular respiration quiz twice, and Mr. Banerjee had offered him a strange bargain: spend Saturday mornings at the community garden until he could trace glucose all the way to ATP, out loud, without notes. Hudson had expected worksheets. Instead Mr. Banerjee handed him a trowel and put him to work turning the compost, saying only that the soil would teach him patience if the biochemistry would not.

The garden sat behind the shuttered elementary school, three dozen plots fenced in chain link, and on the first Saturday Hudson found he was not alone. George was there because his mother had requisitioned his weekends as repayment for a cracked windshield, and Laiba was there because she actually liked it, which Hudson found suspicious in a person their age.

"Honestly it's not that hard," Laiba said, thinning carrots in the next plot over. "Glycolysis, Krebs cycle, then the electron transport chain. It's a relay."

"I know the words," Hudson said. "I can recite the words. I just don't get how it actually makes ATP. Like, where does the energy physically come from at the end?" He stabbed the trowel into the dirt harder than the dirt deserved.

George, who was hauling a hose across the path, paused. "You know what this reminds me of? My uncle's farm upstate. They've got a creek and a little dam, and a turbine underneath. Water stacks up behind the dam, then they let it rush through and it spins the thing. Generates power for half the barn."

"That's a turbine," Hudson said. "Cells don't have turbines."

"Cells don't have anything," George said. "They're like, soup. That's what I never got."

The following Saturday Mr. Banerjee assigned them to repair the irrigation line at the far end of the garden, where an old rain barrel fed a drip system down a gentle slope. The barrel had cracked over the winter. As they worked, Hudson noticed something: the plots at the bottom of the slope, the ones nearest the outlet, were lush and dark, while the plots uphill were pale and struggling. Water pressure, he thought. The water piled up in the high barrel, and the whole line downstream depended on that difference between the top and the bottom.

He sat back on his heels. "George. That dam thing you said."

"What about it?"

"There's a buildup on one side and not the other, and the flow through is what does the work." He was talking faster now, half to himself. "In the mitochondria. What if the electrons don't make ATP directly. What if they pump something across a membrane, and it piles up on one side, like water behind a wall, and then it flows back through and that flow is what actually makes the ATP?"

"Protons," Laiba said from two rows over, where she had been listening while pulling weeds, jaundiced and skeptical as she always was about Hudson's flashes of insight. "It's protons, if you're going where I think you're going. There's a name for it. Chemiosmosis."

"I've never seen that word," Hudson said.

"It's not really in our textbook. Some guy came up with it way back. My sister did a paper on him."

Mr. Banerjee came down the path with a coil of spare tubing over his shoulder, and Hudson, wary of being told the answer, asked Laiba quietly for the details before the adult could arrive and turn it into a lesson.

"Peter Mitchell," Laiba said. "1961. He proposed that cells make ATP using a proton gradient across a membrane. He won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for it in 1978."

"Seventeen years later," Hudson said. "They made him wait seventeen years?"

"People thought he was wrong for a long time. It was too weird. Everybody wanted ATP to be made directly, some clean little handoff, not a buildup behind a wall."

Hudson looked at the repaired barrel, the slope, the dark plots at the bottom. He liked the direct version better too. Causality you could hold in your hand, A touching B, instead of this strange arrangement where the energy hid in a difference, in the gap between two sides of a membrane. But the gap explained the part nothing else had explained. It explained why the electrons kept moving down the chain at all. He still couldn't quite picture a proton, and he said so.

"That part I can't give you," Laiba said. "Nobody can. You'll just have to live with it."

On Monday Mr. Banerjee called Hudson to the whiteboard after class and told him to trace it, all of it, glucose to ATP, no notes. Hudson drew the membrane as two parallel lines, drew the pileup on one side like the water behind George's uncle's dam, drew the arrow of flow back through, and heard himself say the word chemiosmosis without stumbling. Mr. Banerjee didn't smile, but he uncapped a marker and wrote a single checkmark beside the diagram, then a second one, and slid the marker across the desk toward him.

"One more thing," Mr. Banerjee said. "Draw me where the protons are when the cell runs out of glucose."

activity: the language of contracts and forms, such as terms, conditions, liability, consent and signatures
knowledge_domain: the language of contracts and forms, such as terms, conditions, liability, consent and signatures
fact: Under English common law, consideration must have some value but need not be a fair price; courts do not generally judge whether a bargain was a good one.
story:
The queue at the rental counter moved slowly, which gave Victoria time to read the laminated card taped to the desk. Terms and conditions applied. The driver assumed full liability for damage, theft and vandalism. A signature constituted consent to all clauses above and below the line. She was seventeen and therefore invisible to the whole apparatus, standing beside her father while he handled the paperwork for the car that would carry them to her college interview, and she found she did not mind being invisible. It was restful, watching a contract from the outside.

Atticus stood with them because his own father had been sequestered at a conference all week and had asked, by text, that Atticus tag along and be driven home. He had been quiet since the motorway, and now, in the flat light of the terminal, he leaned close to Victoria and said, "I did something stupid."

"You say that weekly."

"I sold my bike. To the guy who fixes the boilers on our street. Twenty quid."

The desk agent, a woman whose badge read Ms. Singh, was clicking through a screen at her own unhurried pace. Behind them, a saturnine man in a grey suit waited with his hands folded, radiating the patience of someone who had decided long ago that nothing in an airport was worth hurrying for.

"It's worth two hundred," Atticus said. "Easy. I looked it up last night. He knew that. He's fixed it, I've seen him riding it. Can I undo it? There's no signature, nothing in writing. It was just cash and a handshake."

Victoria turned the question over while her father initialed a box accepting liability for the windscreen, then a second box declining the waiver, then a third whose purpose nobody explained. Consent, in this place, was a series of small marks. She thought about the handshake, which had felt so clean at the time, so final in a way that signing things never quite did.

"Ms. Singh," she said, surprising herself. "Hypothetically. Someone sells something for way less than it's worth. Can they get out of it later?"

Ms. Singh did not look up from the keyboard. "Under English common law, consideration only has to have some value. It doesn't have to be a fair price. Courts don't judge whether a bargain was a good one." She slid a form across the desk to Victoria's father. "You'd want to ask a magistrate in the actual case, of course, or a solicitor, but that's the principle as I understand it."

"So the twenty quid counts," Victoria said.

"The twenty quid counts. It's ugly, but it counts."

Atticus exhaled through his teeth. "Great. So I'm the guy who sold a two-hundred-pound bike for twenty and no magistrate anywhere is going to rescue me from my own handshake." He said it lightly enough, but his hands were in his pockets and his shoulders had dropped a centimetre, the way they did when he lost a match he had spent weeks preparing for. Victoria understood the shape of it, though not the whole of it: his parents' divorce had made him newly careful about things that could not be taken back, and this felt to him like one more door closing softly behind him. She wanted to say something about lessons, about how everyone overpays for something at seventeen, and then decided he would hear the falseness in it better than she would.

Her father was signing now, the pen scratching through the last page, and Ms. Singh was reciting something about fuel levels and tolls, and the saturnine man behind them shifted his weight with a small sigh. Victoria held out the pen afterwards and took it back to return it, and in the pocket of the moment Atticus's phone buzzed. He read the screen, and his face opened. "It's him. The boiler guy. He says his sister's visiting and she already has a bike, and he feels bad about the price, and would I take it back for what he paid." Atticus was already typing, thumbs moving, and Victoria opened her mouth to say wait, think, you don't have to answer this second, but he hit send before the words reached the air.

"Done," he said. "Sold. I mean, bought."

Ms. Singh held up the keys. "Silver estate, bay fourteen. Full to full. And the agreement binds on signature, so no changing your minds now."

Atticus looked at his phone again, then at Victoria, and the boiler man's next message was already on the screen. He turned it toward her so she could read it herself: sure thing, mate, and honestly, I'd have felt bad keeping it at that price, though if you ever want to sell it back to me for twenty, the offer stands.

activity: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
knowledge_domain: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
fact: If the forward reaction is endothermic, raising the temperature shifts the equilibrium toward the products.
story:
The gymnasium smelled of hot glue and floor wax, and Luca had spent forty minutes acclimating to the noise of three hundred people pretending to be interested in other people's volcanoes. His own table held a cooler, a heating pad, three flasks of pale violet solution, and a hand-lettered sign he had rewritten twice on the bus: WHERE DOES THE HEAT GO?

"You're going to lose," Maximiliano said, leaning against the table with the confidence of someone whose own project was a poster about compost. "Hanna's at table nine with the coral thing. Coral. Judges love coral."

"Judges love data."

"Then you're both doomed."

The reaction in Luca's flasks was one he had found in a library book, the kind with a cracked spine and someone's sandwich grease on page 112, and it had a property he liked: it sat at equilibrium, going forward and backward at once, visibly the same. Until you changed the temperature. Then it moved. He had a theory about which way. He also had Hanna, who had the opposite theory, and she was already crossing the gym toward him with her laconic stride, hands in the pockets of her blazer, the way she walked when she had decided something and wanted you to ask what.

"Cooled one yet?" she said.

"Not yet. Waiting for the judge."

"If you cool it and it goes darker, I win."

"And if it goes lighter, I win, and you owe me a croissant."

"You hate croissants."

"I hate losing more than I hate croissants."

The bet had started three weeks ago, in Mr. Morales's classroom after sixth period, when Luca had stayed to refill the ice bucket and found Hanna already there, guarding the radiator like it was a nest. She had been warming a sample of the same solution in a water bath, murmuring to it. When he asked what she expected, she had said only, "Watch," and the solution had done something neither of them could agree on afterward, because the bell rang, the flask got knocked, and the moment was gone. That was the trouble with equilibrium. It forgave nothing and kept no records.

Mr. Morales, when they had both appealed to him the next morning, had refused to referee. "You want the answer handed to you, do chemistry from a textbook," he said, stacking trays. "You want to know it, run it until it stops surprising you." Then he had smiled in a way that made Luca suspect he knew exactly which of them was right and found the withholding funny.

So the science fair had become the arbiter by default. Luca had spent the week apportioning his sample into sealed flasks, labeling them A through F, planning a demonstration clean enough that even Maximiliano could not accuse him of thumb-on-the-scale. Ice bath for one, heating pad for another, one held at room temperature as the control, which was currently just sitting there being purple, radiating an air of managerial neutrality.

At ten-fifteen, a judge arrived, a woman with a clipboard and a lanyard that said DR. OKAFOR. She looked at the sign, then at the flasks, then at Luca.

"Talk to me," she said.

"So this system is at equilibrium," Luca began, and behind him he heard the squeak of Hanna's sneakers as she materialized, because of course she did. "Both directions are happening at once. My claim is about what happens when I heat it."

"His claim," Hanna said, "is backwards."

Dr. Okafor's eyebrows went up a pleasant half-centimeter. "Well. Heat one."

This was the moment Luca had rehearsed, and his hands were less steady than the rehearsal. He set flask B on the heating pad and turned the dial. The solution sat there. Maximiliano, who had drifted back, said, "It's doing nothing, this is humiliating," and Hanna said, "Shh," without taking her eyes off it, and Luca realized his own theory had a hole in it he had never once examined. He knew which way he wanted it to shift. He had never actually confirmed which direction of the reaction soaked up the heat in the first place. The library book had mentioned it in one clause on a greasy page, and he had read it at eleven at night, and now, watching the violet, he could not remember if the clause had said the forward reaction was endothermic or the reverse one was.

The solution lightened. Visibly, gradually, like the color deciding to leave. Luca exhaled.

"It shifted toward the products," he said slowly, testing each word as it came out. "Which means the forward reaction has to be the one that takes in the heat. It's endothermic." He looked at Hanna, whose mouth had opened and shut. "Raising the temperature pushed it toward the products because forward absorbs the heat. I had it right, but for the reason I only just now actually have."

"So I owe you a croissant you hate," Hanna said.

"You owe me a croissant I've earned."

Dr. Okafor was writing something, and Luca could not see what, and the ice bath sat untouched at the end of the table, waiting for the question she had not yet asked.

"Cool it," she said.

activity: argument structures, nuanced reasoning and conditional thinking in abstract and hypothetical discussion
knowledge_domain: argument structures, nuanced reasoning and conditional thinking in abstract and hypothetical discussion
fact: Steelmanning is the practice of restating an opposing argument in its strongest form, even stronger than the other person put it, before responding to it.
story:
The philosophy classroom smelled of whiteboard marker and radiator dust, and Simon had chosen a seat near the window because the afternoon light made it easier to look like he was thinking. Mr. Dhillon wrote a single sentence on the board: Should the school ban phones entirely? He did not turn around while he wrote, and when he did turn, he said only, "Pick a side. You have four minutes to prepare the strongest case you can. Andreanne, Simon, you two will argue against each other."

Simon drew the pro-ban position out of the cup Matheo was holding, unfolded the slip, and felt the small deflation of having to defend something he did not believe. He scribbled points anyway: distraction, sleep, the engineered pull of apps. When the four minutes ended, Andreanne went first. She said phones were how students with jobs and siblings and buses actually held their lives together, and that banning them punished the poorest kids first. Simon listened with half his attention, waiting for his turn, and when it came he said, "Phones make you distracted, though. Everyone knows that." It came out flat, and he heard it come out flat, and he kept going anyway because stopping felt worse.

"That's not what I said," Andreanne said. "I didn't say phones make you focused. I said a ban lands unevenly." Mr. Dhillon did not intervene. He was leaning against the radiator with his arms folded, watching Simon the way the coach watched you after a bad first set, and Matheo, two rows back, said, "You knocked over a scarecrow, man. That's not her argument."

Simon felt his face warm. He looked down at his notes, which were useless, and then he did something he had not planned. He said, "Okay. Let me try again." And he began to restate her case, only stronger. He said that a total ban would fall hardest on students whose phones were their only calendars, their only alarm clocks, their only way to reach a parent mid-shift, and that a school claiming to act in loco parentis would be cutting the parent out of the loop it claimed to hold. He built it higher than she had, tilting the argument in her favor until it loomed. "If that's the argument," he said, "then my side has to answer it, not the version I invented." He answered it badly, honestly, and lost the room's vote twelve to five.

Afterward, packing up, Matheo clapped him on the shoulder. "That thing you did at the start, restating her side stronger than she said it before you answered. Mr. Dhillon calls that steelmanning." Simon turned the word over. Steelmanning. He copied it into the margin of his notebook without asking what it meant, because he already knew.

At home that evening the argument he had been avoiding for a week was waiting for him at the kitchen table. His father wanted him home by ten on weekends, citing an incident two Saturdays ago that Simon had explained badly at the time and had let ossify, in the weeks since, into a fixed story about irresponsibility. Simon opened his mouth to say it wasn't fair, and heard, in advance, exactly how it would sound: thin, whiny, the scarecrow again.

So he sat down across from his father and said, "Before I say anything, let me say your side. Tell me if I get it right." His father set down his fork. Simon said that his father worked early shifts, that he could not sleep until he knew the door was locked, that two weeks ago no one had answered texts for ninety minutes and he had imagined the worst, and that trust, once broken in a small way, was harder to rebuild than it was to lose. He said it more strongly than his father had ever said it, and when he finished, the kitchen was quiet and the refrigerator hummed like something only now quiescent.

His father looked at him for a long moment. "Ninety minutes," he said. "You don't know what that was like."

"No," Simon said. "But I can guess. And I'm not going to answer that by telling you I'm sixteen and it's a curfew. You're right that I went dark. That's on me."

From across the table, his father watched the boy he had been arguing with turn into someone else mid-sentence, and he was not sure he liked it, though he could not have said why. It felt like being handed a better version of his own case by the opposing counsel, a move that was either generous or a trap. He had spent enough years in an office where people only ever spoke in order to win, and he recognized the technique now arriving at his own kitchen table, wearing his son's face. "Where did you learn that?" he asked.

"Philosophy class," Simon said. "It's not a trick."

"It feels like one."

"Then tell me where I got your side wrong." Simon slid his own reasoning across the table the way he had watched Andreanne do: the late buses, the fact that his friends' parents let them stay out later, the fact that he was going to be somewhere on his own in two years with no curfew at all and had to learn to come home because he chose to, not because a rule made the choice for him. He laid it out plainly, without heat, and then waited.

His father tapped the table twice, a habit from years of poker with his own brother. "Eleven," he said finally. "Saturdays. And you text at ten thirty, not eleven, so I'm not watching the clock build up something to worry about. If you go dark again, we're back to ten." Simon agreed. He did not feel that he had won, exactly; he was aware that his father might have conceded more to the technique than to him, and that some of what sat between them, the ninety minutes, the two years ahead, the moving out, stayed exactly as uncertain as before. But the door was open and the evening light had gone and his father was still talking, asking about the class, asking what else they argued about there.

"Phones, mostly," Simon said, and got up to rinse his plate.

activity: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
knowledge_domain: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
fact: Capitalization means unpaid interest is added to a loan's principal, so from then on interest is charged on the interest too.
story:
The line at the bank moved slowly, and Caleb counted the floor tiles between himself and the teller windows, eleven, then gave up. In his pocket was the fold of cash from a summer of carting groceries, six hundred and forty dollars, and in his head was the number he wanted it to become. Nikki stood beside him with a withdrawal slip she had filled out in pen so hard it tore the paper.

"You could just keep it in your sock," she said.

"And watch it stay six hundred dollars forever."

"Better than watching it do whatever money does in banks."

The lights dimmed twice, flickered, steadied. Someone at the far counter was arguing in a low voice about a fee, and the sound carried the way small sounds do in quiet rooms, forcing itself into everyone's consciousness whether they consented or not. Caleb leaned toward the window marked New Accounts. A man with a laminated name tag, Mr. Wang, was explaining something to a young woman whose shoulders had gone rigid.

"I borrowed nineteen thousand," the woman said. Not loud. Flat. "Four years ago. I haven't even finished paying the interest yet. How is the balance twenty-two?"

Mr. Wang turned his monitor toward her, and Caleb, close enough now that pretending not to listen required real effort, saw a line graph rising in a shallow, relentless curve.

"Your payments have been covering interest only," Mr. Wang said. "Whatever wasn't paid got added to what you owe."

"Added." She said the word like it had a smell. "So the interest itself owes interest."

"Capitalization," Mr. Wang said. "That's what it's called, when unpaid interest is added to the principal. From then on, interest is charged on the interest too."

Caleb's sister had said almost nothing at dinner last month, only pushed rice around her plate and finally said, my loan is bigger than what I took out, which had made no sense to him then. He had assumed she'd missed payments, been fined, done something. Now the graph's curve answered a question he hadn't known he was holding, and the answer worked in both directions, which was the part that made him cold and awake at once.

When the woman left, clutching her printout, Caleb stepped up. "I want to open a savings account," he said. "And I have a question."

Mr. Wang's eyebrows offered him the floor.

"If the same thing happens in reverse. If the bank pays me interest and I don't take it out. Does it capitalize onto mine the same way?"

Mr. Wang slid a brochure across the counter. "Compounded monthly, on this one. It works the way you're thinking."

"Caleb," Nikki said behind him, "you're doing the thing where you turn into your econ textbook."

"The graph goes up either way." He was writing his name on the application, and his pen slowed. "It went up on her for four years while she thought she was standing still. It can go up for me."

"It can also go nowhere if you requisition half of it for that car you keep showing me on your phone."

"That's not what requisition means."

"It's exactly what it means. You're taking six hundred dollars and marching it off to a guy on Marketplace who called you 'boss' twice in one text."

Mr. Wang was watching them with the mild patience of a man who heard arguments like this every afternoon. Caleb looked at the deposit slip, at the six hundred and forty dollars in his pocket, at the graph still faintly ghosted on the abandoned monitor. His father had called the car a profligate idea, had used the word at the table and then softened it with a shrug, as if to say, but you're eighteen, and eighteen has its own logic. The bus route to campus took fifty minutes each way. A car would take fifteen and cost him, by his rough count, most of what he could earn during the semester, and then gas on top of that, which was interest of a different kind, the kind nobody graphs for you.

He filled out the slip for six hundred and forty dollars, all of it, and before he could hand it over he crossed out the total and wrote five hundred. Nikki saw it over his shoulder.

"Keeping the car alive, then."

"Keeping it possible," Caleb said. "There's a difference."

"A hundred and forty dollars of difference."

"More, if it sits here." He didn't know yet whether he was being shrewd or just frightened, whether the curve on that monitor was a promise or a warning, and he was honest enough with himself to admit that both readings fit the same line. He pushed the deposit slip across the counter. "Five hundred into savings."

Mr. Wang took the slip and began typing, and the printer beside him hummed and produced a receipt, thin and blue, with a balance on it that was, for the moment, exactly what Caleb had given it.

activity: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
knowledge_domain: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
fact: In her 2017 book 'Radical Candor', Kim Scott argues good feedback combines caring personally about someone with challenging them directly.
story:
The porch boards at his grandfather's house still held the afternoon heat, and Oliver sat down on them anyway, phone in his hand, thumb hovering over the message he had drafted and deleted four times since the bus ride home. Everett had played the whole second half on Saturday without saying a word, which was the problem, or the start of it. Their striker, the one everyone called Trix even though her name was Beatrice, had been drifting offside on the same run all season, and Everett, who played the through balls, had seen it and said nothing, and on Saturday it had cost them the county semi-final by a single disallowed goal.

Hayley was sprawled in the wicker chair with her shoes off, reading a book she'd been carrying around all week, some management thing with an orange cover. "You're prevaricating," she said without looking up. "You've typed the same sentence three times. I can hear you not sending it."

"It's not that simple." Oliver turned the phone face down on his knee. "If I tell him he cost us the game, that's just cruel. He already knows we lost. Everybody knows."

Hayley marked her page with a receipt and looked at him properly. "Then don't tell him that. Tell him the true thing underneath it." She held up the book. "This woman Kim Scott, she wrote a whole book about it. In 2017. It's called Radical Candor." She tapped the cover. "The idea is you have to do two things at once. Care about the person, actually care, and challenge them directly. Skip either one and it goes wrong."

"That sounds like something Ms. Clarke-Williams would put on a poster."

"It sounds like something that would have won us the game if anyone had told Trix in October." Hayley put her shoes back on. "Everett was being nice. Nice got us knocked out."

Inside, through the screen door, Oliver's grandfather was at the kitchen table with a dismantled mantel clock in front of him, a jeweler's loupe pushed up on his forehead. Oliver had come here after every loss since he was nine, and the ritual never changed: tea, the clock, the listening. Today the old man was poking at a small brass wheel with a pair of fine pliers, and a beetle had wandered onto the table from somewhere and was making its slow way across the felt mat. "No sentience in that," his grandfather said, nodding at it. "It doesn't know where it's going. It just goes. I sometimes think people confuse motion with purpose." He glanced up. "You've got the look of a boy holding a letter he's afraid to post."

Oliver told him about Everett, and Trix, and the offside run, and how he'd have to see Everett at Monday practice and either say something or keep being what Hayley had called nice. His grandfather set the pliers down and let the beetle walk onto a scrap of paper, then placed it on the windowsill among the geraniums. "Your grandmother could never tell me when I'd cooked something badly," he said. "Forty years of paprika. I only found out from your aunt." He picked the pliers up again. "The kindest thing anyone ever said to me was your mother, telling me I was wrong about something and staying in the room afterward."

On Monday the gym smelled of floor wax and old sweat, and Everett was reticent in the way Oliver had learned to read over three years of sharing a changing room: shoulders up, answering in half sentences, packing his bag like the locker owed him money. Oliver waited until the others had drifted toward the doors, then sat on the bench beside him and said, "Can I tell you something about Saturday? It's not about the loss."

Everett went still, one shoe in his hand.

"You're the best passer on the team, and you see things nobody else sees, and I know you knew Trix was drifting offside, because I watched you check the line twice before the through ball. You didn't tell her, and I think you didn't because you didn't want to hurt her. But you're good enough that staying quiet actually hurts us." Oliver heard his own voice shake slightly on the last part and kept going anyway. "If you'd told her in October, she'd have fixed it by December. That's all. I'm telling you because I want us to be good together, not because I'm blaming you."

Everett laced his shoe very slowly. When he finally spoke, it was to the laces. "I told her. In October. Twice." He stood and pulled his bag up onto his shoulder. "She said she'd fix it. She didn't, and I didn't know how to say it again without sounding like I was riding her." He looked at Oliver then, and something in his face had loosened, almost amused. "So go tell her. Third time. Apparently you're the one who's good at this now."

Across the gym, Trix was the last one out, holding the door open with her hip, and Oliver got up and went after her before he could think of a single reason not to.

activity: to debate a current issue entirely in a new language for five minutes
knowledge_domain: to debate a current issue entirely in a new language for five minutes
fact: False friends are words that look alike in two languages but differ in meaning; Spanish 'embarazada' means pregnant, not embarrassed.
story:
Jolene's kitchen smelled of burnt toast and lemon dish soap, and the table had been cleared to make room for three laptops, a legal pad, and a bowl of grapes nobody was eating. Ryder sat with his Spanish vocabulary list curled at the corners, running his thumb along the edge until the paper went soft. In eight days he had to debate water rights for five minutes, entirely in Spanish, in front of his whole class, and so far he could manage about forty seconds before his mind went white.

"Toma," Jolene said, sliding a glass of water across the table. "You're muttering in English again. That's cheating."

"Practicing isn't cheating." He drank anyway. The water tasted faintly of the pipes, metallic and cold.

Cyril arrived late, as he always did, carrying his backpack on one shoulder and an unshaken confidence that Ryder had envied since seventh grade. Cyril had spent two summers in Oaxaca with his cousins and spoke with an ease that made Spanish sound like breathing. He dropped into the fourth chair and pulled the legal pad toward himself. "Okay. Topic: quien controla el agua del río. Who controls the river's water. You're the farmer. I'm the city. Go."

Ryder started, haltingly, his voice thin in the small room. He had facts he wanted, about the river corridor and the farms that depended on it, and he reached for the word he'd found the night before, the one that meant the green land along a riverbank, lush and necessary. "Los granjeros necesitan la zona riparia," he said, "porque..." He lost the thread of the sentence, found it, lost it again. Cyril listened without laughing, which was somehow worse than laughing, because Ryder could see him assembling corrections behind his eyes.

"You said embarazada," Cyril said, finally. "Twice."

"I said the farmers are embarrassed about the water shortage. Embarrassed. It's the same word."

"It's not." Cyril leaned back until the chair creaked. "They're false friends. Words that look alike in two languages but mean different things. Embarazada means pregnant. You told the class the farmers are pregnant."

Ryder stared at him. The clock above the stove ticked through several full seconds. Then Jolene made a small sound through her nose, trying to hold it in, and failed, and then all three of them were laughing, hard enough that Ryder had to set the water down before he spilled it. When he caught his breath his face was still hot, but something in his chest had loosened. The mistake was out in the air now. It belonged to the room and not to him.

They drilled for another hour. Jolene, who knew no Spanish at all, held up the vocabulary cards and rated his delivery on a scale she invented on the spot, from "funeral" to "weatherman." Cyril made him argue the city's side too, then the environmental agency's, then back to the farmer, until Ryder could feel the shape of the disagreement from the inside. That was the part nobody had told him about debating: it wasn't about winning. He had walked in wanting to defeat Cyril, and somewhere between the third and sixth round he found himself saying, in his creaking Spanish, that the farmer's claim was strong but not absolute, that the river belonged to everyone and therefore fully to no one. He wasn't sure he believed it. He wasn't sure he didn't. Cyril nodded slowly, the way he did when a point landed, and Ryder felt a flicker of something like acumen, borrowed but real, settling briefly in him like a bird on a wire.

At dusk they moved to the back porch, where the wind moved through the neighbor's tall grass in slow waves, making the whole yard undulate as if it were water, which struck Ryder as either ironic or appropriate given the topic. Ms. Otieno, the neighbor on the other side, was watering her roses and called over the fence to ask what language they were butchering. "Español," Ryder called back, and she raised her hose in salute.

On Monday he stood at the front of the classroom and spoke for four minutes and fifty seconds. He used zona riparia correctly. He argued the farmer's side with the concession built in, that the claim was strong but the river answered to others too. And in the last minute, reaching for a closing flourish, he said embarazada again, on purpose this time, paused, and corrected himself, and the class roared. Some of the laughter was at him. He could hear which part was, and it stung even as he smiled. He had wanted to be flawless, and instead he was memorable. As he sat down, Ms. Otieno wrote something in her grade book without looking up, and Ryder watched the pen move until he couldn't read it anymore.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: Water boils at a lower temperature at high altitude, about 95 degrees Celsius at 5,000 feet, so boiled foods take longer to cook.
story:
The pasta box in Nathaniel's hand had a cooking time printed on the back, eleven minutes, and he did not believe it anymore. He stood in aisle four of the mountain-town grocery with his phone showing a text from his mother: working double, home by ten, there's money in the jar. His little brother was home with the sitter, and the first pot of spaghetti, drained forty minutes ago, had come out hard in the middle, chalky, wrong. He had followed the box exactly. He had set a timer. The evidence and the instructions contradicted each other, and only one of them was lying.

"You're back," said Josue, restocking cans two shelves down in his green apron. "That's twice in one night, and you looked mad the first time."

"The spaghetti didn't cook." Nathaniel held up the new box like an exhibit. "Eleven minutes, it said. I gave it fourteen to be safe. It was like biting a shoelace."

Josue came over and squinted at the directions. "Maxx's family never cooks pasta," he said. "They say it's cursed. They came up from the valley two years ago and his mom swears nothing boils right anymore. She calls it the mountain tax."

Nathaniel almost laughed, but the phrase snagged on something. The mountain tax. Last summer, at the lake campsite above town, his father had boiled eggs for twelve minutes and they came out runny, and his uncle had shrugged and said the water was weird up here. At the time Nathaniel had filed it under family superstition, alongside his grandmother's insistence that pasta was done when it stuck to the wall. Two ways of thinking about the same problem: the box's precision, and the older, looser wisdom that said trust the food, not the clock. He had dismissed the second as unscientific. Now the first had failed him too, publicly, in front of a seven-year-old who had asked for spaghetti and received shoelaces.

"I need the computer in the school library," he said, then remembered it was Friday night. He typed into his phone instead, standing between the canned tomatoes and the olive oil: does water boil differently at high altitude. The answer came back and he read it twice. Water boils at a lower temperature at high altitude, about 95 degrees Celsius at 5,000 feet, so boiled foods take longer to cook. He looked up. Josue was watching him with the patience of someone paid by the hour.

"Ninety-five degrees," Nathaniel said. "That's it. That's the tax." He said it the way his uncle might have, half joking, but the number underneath was exact, and exactness was what he'd been missing. The water wasn't broken; it was doing precisely what physics asked of it at this elevation, and the box, written for kitchens at sea level, simply didn't know where Nathaniel lived.

At the register, Mr. Ionescu, who kept the garden three houses down and worked the registers on weekends, rang up the pasta and a bag of salt. "Twice tonight," he observed, tapping the box. His comments were usually incisive and never explained, a habit Nathaniel had found unsettling until he understood it was respect. "Cooking for the family?"

"Trying to," Nathaniel said. "My mom's on a double." He hesitated, then decided the man had earned the whole truth. "First batch came out hard. I figured out why, though." He laid out the altitude, the boiling point, the longer cooking, all of it in two sentences, and Mr. Ionescu nodded slowly, as if confirming something he'd suspected about water for decades.

"Then cook it longer and taste as you go," Mr. Ionescu said, sliding the bag across. "Old people and science agreeing for once. Write that down."

At home the sitter had already left a note about the disaster pasta, and his brother was at the table drawing what appeared to be a shark eating spaghetti. Nathaniel filled the pot, salted the water, and did not set a timer. Instead he fished out a strand every minute past the box's number and bit it, holding each one up to the light like a small experiment, the tasting becoming a kind of leitmotif for the evening, again and again until the chalk gave way to gold. His grandmother's wall trick surfaced in his mind and he tried that too, and the strand stuck, which proved nothing scientifically and everything practically. He still wasn't sure which method was truth and which was luck; possibly the honest answer was that the box knew one thing, the mountain knew another, and he had to stand between them and taste.

At twelve minutes past the printed time, he drained the pot, ladled the sauce, and set the plate in front of his brother, who looked at it with the wariness of someone recently betrayed. Nathaniel cut a piece of pasta in half and held out the cross-section first, pale and soft all the way through. "Different batch," he said. "Different rules up here."

His brother took the fork.

activity: applying to college and waiting for the answer
knowledge_domain: applying to college and waiting for the answer
fact: Need-blind admission means a college decides whom to admit without considering whether the applicant can afford to pay; many US colleges are instead need-aware.
story:
The mailbox at the end of Owen's driveway had a dented lid that stuck in humid weather, and every afternoon at four he pried it open with both hands, looked inside, and closed it again. Today there was something: a thick envelope from Hartwell College, the safety school three states away, offering him a merit scholarship of eight thousand dollars a year. He read it standing in the gravel, and then he read it again, because eight thousand dollars against a tuition of fifty-two thousand left a shape he could not make fit anything.

He carried the envelope inside, where his mother was folding laundry at the kitchen table. She asked what it was, and when he told her she said, "That's something, at least," in the voice she used when the numbers were against them and she did not want to say so. Their expected contribution, according to the federal form they had filled out in February, was four thousand dollars a year. The gap was not the kind of thing you could close by working summers at the garden center, which Owen had done for two years and which paid eleven dollars an hour.

At school the next morning he found Alexa at her locker and showed her the letter. She was the one person he knew who had done the same research he had, late at night, with the family laptop propped on a chemistry textbook.

"Which ones on your list are need-blind?" she asked, and he had to admit he hadn't made a list, exactly, just a stack of brochures arranged by how much he liked the photographs. "Need-blind means they decide who gets in without looking at whether you can pay," she said, shutting her locker. "A lot of places aren't like that. They're need-aware, so if you need a lot of aid, it can count against you when they're deciding." She pulled a folded printout from her backpack, a grid she'd made with three columns: school, deadline, and whether the admissions office looked at finances when it made its decisions. Two of her schools did not. Five did.

Owen thought of Ridgemont, the small school two hours north with the writing program he wanted, the one he had visited last October. He remembered standing in the admissions lobby while a woman with a florid scarf explained the early decision option, and his father asking, quietly, in the parking lot afterward, whether applying early meant committing to the cost before they knew the aid. His father had been laid off that spring; the visit had been paid for with the last of the vacation fund. Owen had applied early anyway, regular decision, because the early option required a signed commitment to attend, an injunction his father refused to give without knowing the price. Since December, Ridgemont had said only that his file was under review.

That night he looked up Ridgemont's admissions page and found, four screens down, a line stating that the college was need-aware in its admissions process. He sat for a while with his hands flat on the desk. It did not mean he was rejected, and it did not mean he was poor, though he understood that in this context it meant something adjacent to poor. It meant that when the committee sat down with his file, his parents' four-thousand-dollar contribution was on the table next to his essay, and he could not know which one weighed more, or whether the waiting would end in a thin envelope either way.

He remonstrated with himself for twenty minutes, out loud, pacing the hallway outside his room: he should have checked in October, he should have asked Alexa in November, he should have understood that the brochures with their photographs of quadrangles in autumn were designed by people whose job it was to make him want something. Then he stopped, because blaming himself in the hallway did not change the deadline situation, and there were, Alexa's grid said, eleven days left before one of the need-blind schools on her list closed its regular application.

The problem was the essay. The school, called Bannister, required a response to a prompt about a belief he had changed his mind about, and Owen had nothing drafted. He called Charles, who had applied to Bannister in December and been deferred, and Charles talked him through the prompt for forty minutes while Owen typed. Owen wrote about the belief, held since childhood, that admitting you needed help cost you something you could not get back; he wrote about the federal form, and his father's voice in the parking lot, and the difference between the two kinds of colleges on Alexa's grid. It was not his best writing. It was true, and it was submitted at 11:42 that night, with eightteen minutes to spare.

The next afternoon, Mr. Chan was trimming his hedge across the street when Owen walked down to the mailbox with a certified mail receipt in his hand, the paper record of a transcript request he had driven to the school office to sign that morning. Mr. Chan asked how the college search was going, and Owen told him: one offer, one silence, one new application in the air. Mr. Chan nodded and said that his own son, years ago, had chosen the school that answered first. Owen said he wasn't going to do that. He pried open the dented lid, found the box empty, and stood there holding it ajar, looking down the street toward the corner where the mail truck turned in.

activity: to calculate the moles of a product formed from a given mass of reactant using molar mass
knowledge_domain: to calculate the moles of a product formed from a given mass of reactant using molar mass
fact: Percent yield is the actual mass of product obtained divided by the theoretical yield, multiplied by 100.
story:
The crystals sat in a shallow dish on the kitchen table, grey-white and clustered like something igneous that had no business forming in a saucepan. Maika had grown them over eleven days for the science fair, and this morning, when she tipped them out onto the filter paper and weighed them, the number on the scale had made her stomach drop. The crystals weighed less than the sheet of paper had led her to expect. A lot less.

She had the kitchen to herself until six. Her mother was on the early shift, and the counter was still dusted with the alum powder she had measured out on Sunday, a faint salt-smell hanging over it. Maika spread her notebook open between the fruit bowl and the stove and found the page where she had written the recipe: so many grams of alum, dissolved in hot water, cooled slowly. Somewhere in her binder was the chemistry Ms. López had drilled into them before the fair, the long ladder of a calculation that turned grams into moles and moles into grams again, using molar mass as the rungs. She had done it once for homework and gotten it right by accident, she suspected. Now it mattered.

Clare arrived first, still in her track pants, carrying two cans of soda and a grudge. "The coach benched me the whole second half," she said, dropping into the chair opposite. "He said missing practice has consequences. Like deterrence, except it doesn't work, because I was at the dentist." She cracked a can and looked at the dish. "Those are your crystals? They look like gravel."

"They're supposed to look like that," Maika said, though she wasn't sure they were supposed to look quite like that. She copied the mass of alum she had started with into a fresh column and began the climb: grams of reactant, divided by its molar mass, which she looked up on the printed table Ms. López had given them, and then moles of reactant becoming moles of product, one for one, and then moles multiplied back into grams using the molar mass of the product. The arithmetic was slow because she refused to rush it. When she reached the bottom of the ladder she sat back. The theoretical yield, if everything had gone the way the numbers said it should, was more than double what her dish held.

Lilly let herself in through the back door without knocking, the way she had since they were nine. "Ms. López said you were panicking about the fair," she said, peering at the page. "She said, and I quote, tell her the numbers are telling her something."

"The numbers are telling me I failed." Maika turned the notebook so Lilly could see. "I did the whole thing. Started with this much, ended with half of what I should have. That's the whole project in the bin."

Clare leaned over Lilly's shoulder. She was the one of them who took chemistry seriously only when it involved fire. "Wait, though," she said slowly. "Failed, or did some of it not come out?" Maika opened her mouth to say it was the same thing, and then didn't. Some of the alum might still be dissolved in the water she had poured off. Some might have stayed behind in the saucepan, that thin frost she had rinsed away without thinking. The crystals themselves were real; they were sitting right there in the dish. What was missing wasn't nothing. It was the difference between what should have formed and what did.

She pulled the calculator toward her and wrote the actual mass at the top of a new line. Below it she wrote the theoretical yield, the number she had earned through the whole slow ladder. "You divide what you got by what you should have gotten," she said, half to herself, "and multiply by a hundred." Clare watched her thumb the keys. "It's called percent yield," Maika said, when the number came up on the screen. She wrote the two words beside it and underlined them once, not twice, because once felt like fact and twice felt like drama.

The percentage was low, and she let it sit on the page while Lilly rinsed the saucepan and Clare read the recipe over again, lips moving. "You poured the leftover liquid down the sink," Clare said. "Sunday. I remember, you made a joke about it." Maika remembered the joke and not the pouring, which was its own small indictment. She was honest enough with herself to hold both things at once: the crystals in the dish were genuinely hers, grown from her own patience, and the loss was genuinely hers too, and there was no way to know from here how much of the missing half had gone down the drain, how much clung to the pan, how much simply never formed. She couldn't run it again before the fair. What she could do was stand in front of the table on Saturday with her low number and say, this is how much I got, and this is how much the math promised, and this gap is the interesting part.

She started a new page titled Results and Discussion, and under Discussion she wrote the first true sentence of the section: some product was lost, and the percent yield records exactly how much. Lilly dried the saucepan and set it back on the stove. Clare drained her soda and stacked the empty can on top of Maika's chemistry binder, right on the corner, so it wouldn't blow away from the fan.

"Don't move that," Maika said, reaching across the table, and slid the binder out from under the can, crystals glinting in the dish between them.

activity: professional tone, structured writing and respectful disagreement in formal communication
knowledge_domain: professional tone, structured writing and respectful disagreement in formal communication
fact: 'Bottom Line Up Front', or BLUF, is a US military writing standard that puts the main point or request in the first lines of a message, before the supporting details.
story:
The volunteer office at the community center smelled of toner and old coffee, and the radiator under the window ticked like a slow clock. Addison had been coming every Tuesday since September, mostly to file donation records, but today Mr. Pierre had slid a laptop across the desk toward her and asked her to draft the email he had been avoiding all week. The city council wanted a summary of the center's winter coat drive, and he wanted it sent by five o'clock. "You write clean," he said, which was the closest thing to a compliment he ever gave, and then he disappeared into the back room to argue with the copier.

She had his notes, which were less notes than a weather system of worries: attendance figures, a complaint from a donor about drop-off hours, an idea about expanding the drive to two more schools, and buried somewhere near the bottom, the actual request, which was that the council approve an extension of the drop-off deadline by ten days. Addison read the notes twice and felt the problem the way you feel a stone in a shoe. The request, the one thing the council actually had to act on, was hiding under three paragraphs of context that only made sense if you already worked here.

Mateo, who volunteered on Tuesdays too and had a younger brother in Mr. Pierre's evening program, leaned over from the next desk. He was eating sunflower seeds one at a time, a mannerism so constant that the shell fragments on his desk had formed a small landscape. "What's wrong with your face," he said, which was his way of asking what she was thinking.

"I can't find where the email should start," Addison said. "Everything's important and nothing's first." She turned the laptop so he could see Mr. Pierre's notes, the request for the extension sitting in the fourth paragraph like a guest who'd arrived after dinner.

Mateo cracked a seed between his teeth, unhurried. "My cousin's in the Army," he said. "She says they write everything with the main point in the first line or two, before any of the details. It's called BLUF, 'Bottom Line Up Front'. It's a US military writing standard." He brushed a shell fragment off the keyboard. "She says nobody above her has time to hunt for the point."

Addison sat with that for a moment. It sounded blunt at first, almost rude, the opposite of how she'd been taught to ease into a request with appreciation and background. But she thought about the council members, the dozens of emails they must open every morning, and about her own habit of skimming the first lines and deciding from those whether to keep reading. Maybe the polite thing wasn't the long warm-up. Maybe the respectful thing was to value their time enough to say immediately what she needed from them.

She started a new draft. The first line stated the request plainly: the center asked the council to extend the coat drive drop-off deadline by ten days. Then, in order of how much the reader would need them, came the attendance numbers, the current deadline, the two schools that had asked to join late. She kept the donor's complaint about drop-off hours but moved it to a short final section, framed not as a grievance but as a scheduling question the extension might partly solve. When she was done she read it aloud in a low voice, and Mateo listened with his chin propped on his fist, cracking another seed.

"It's weird," he said. "It's shorter but it sounds more serious."

Mr. Pierre came back with toner dust on one sleeve and read the draft standing up, one hand on the edge of the desk. His expression stayed noncommittal for most of it, which Addison had learned was simply his face when he was concentrating, and she caught herself trying to propitiate him before he'd said anything, already composing a defense of the structure in her head. But when he reached the second paragraph he said, "Good, the numbers are where they should be," and when he finished he sat down and made one change, softening a single phrase in the opening so the request asked rather than demanded. Addison watched him do it and decided she'd been wrong to think of BLUF as blunt. The structure held the firmness, which meant the words themselves could afford to be courteous.

There was still the question she couldn't settle, and she said so to Mateo while she waited for Mr. Pierre to press send. "I don't know if it works on everyone," she said. "Some people might read a request that comes first as pushy. Or the details might matter more to them than we think." She pulled her jacket off the back of the chair. The radiatior ticked on, the copier had gone quiet at last, and through the window the parking lot lights were coming on, one after another, along the row.

"That's the answer to your face question from earlier," Mateo said, and dropped another shell into the small landscape on his desk.

activity: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
knowledge_domain: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
fact: The journal Nature rejected Hans Krebs's 1937 paper on the citric acid cycle, and he published it in the journal Enzymologia instead.
story:
Jason had spread the poster board across two lawn chairs, and the diagram on it looked like a subway map drawn by someone who hated passengers. Glycolysis here, the Krebs cycle there, a scribbled arrow labeled "electron transport chain, probably." Tomorrow morning, seventh period, Mr. Sultani's make-up exam. He had one night.

Lennon dropped through the gap in the fence the way she always did, without asking, holding two cans of root beer and her own crumpled study sheet. Judah came around the front instead, knocking on the gate like a person who believed in gates, which Jason had always found funny given the fence had a hole in it you could drive a bike through.

"Biochem marathon?" Lennon asked, folding herself onto the picnic table.

"Respiration," Jason said. "Glucose to ATP. I have to trace the whole thing and I keep losing the middle. I get glucose broken into pyruvate, fine, and then the diagram turns into spaghetti."

Judah sat down heavily, the way he did when he was carrying news. He had been carrying it since fourth period, apparently, because the first thing out of his mouth was, "The regional committee rejected my entry. The whole science fair project. Rejected."

Lennon opened a root beer and passed it to him, which was her version of condolences. Jason felt the unfairness of it in his own chest, because Judah had spent six weeks on that project, measuring algae growth under different light spectra, and the rejection email had been three sentences long. Judah read it out loud from his phone, and the third sentence was the one that stung, the one about how the entry "did not meet the standard of significance."

"Significance," Judah repeated, like the word had personally insulted his mother. "They can reject you and then tell you it's because you don't matter. That's a whole genre of cruelty."

Jason didn't say anything sympathetic, because Judah hated sympathy, so he did the other thing he did when a friend got knocked down, which was to pick up his phone and start looking for ammunition. It was a habit his mother called arguing like a lawyer and his father called being seventeen. He typed "famous rejected science" with one thumb while Lennon dragged the poster board toward herself and squinted at it.

"Okay, so here's your problem," she said, tapping the middle of the map. "You've drawn the mitochondria like a bean with nothing inside it. The Krebs cycle happens in there, in the matrix, and you've just written 'Krebs???' like it's a cryptid."

"It is a cryptid," Jason said. "It has too many steps and every step has a different enzyme."

His phone buzzed with results. He read one twice, then turned the screen so Judah could see it. "The journal Nature rejected Hans Krebs's 1937 paper on the citric acid cycle. He published it in the journal Enzymologia instead."

Judah took the phone and read it himself, slowly, the way he read anything that might be too good to be true. "The guy the cycle is named after."

"The guy your entire test is named after," Lennon said, pointing at the poster board, and for a second all three of them looked at the scribbled bean as if Krebs himself might climb out of it.

"Nature said no," Judah said. He handed the phone back. He didn't smile exactly, but something in his shoulders let go an inch.

Jason sat with that for a moment, because it did something odd to his own thinking. He had been treating the exam like a verdict, one number on one morning that would declare whether he was a science person or not, and here was evidence that the whole enterprise had always included people saying no to work that turned out to be worth a Nobel Prize. But he also knew, honestly, that he couldn't take too much comfort from it, because Krebs being right didn't mean every rejected thing was secretly a masterpiece. Judah's algae project might be great. It might also need another year. There was no way to know from the rejection alone, and pretending otherwise would just be a kinder way of lying to his friend. He tried to say some of this out loud and it came out as, "It doesn't mean they were wrong about you. It means they might have been. Those aren't the same thing."

"That is the most depressing pep talk in history," Lennon said. "Also you still don't know the cycle. If you fail tomorrow this whole conversation becomes ironic instead of inspiring."

So they drilled. Lennon made Judah hold up the poster like a flashcard while she fired questions, and Judah, who needed the distraction as much as Jason needed the facts, turned out to be merciless about it. Citrate to isocitrate, isocitrate to alpha-ketoglutarate, and every time Jason stalled, Judah said "rejected," which was a terrible mnemonic and worked anyway. At one point Lennon called their whole setup a dialectic, Jason insisting he'd never remember it, Judah insisting he would, and the truth getting made somewhere in between. When Jason complained that his tenth-grade notes were basically obsolescent, Judah said his entire brain was obsolescent, and Mr. Sultani's porch light came on across the fence, and the old man's silhouette appeared at his railing holding a cup of tea.

"Who is being murdered over there?" Mr. Sultani called.

"Cellular respiration," Jason called back.

"Good," Mr. Sultani said. "It has it coming." His porch light stayed on, which Jason chose to read as a kind of blessing, and under it they kept going, Judah quizzing, Lennon correcting, the citric acid cycle turning and turning on its cheap poster board, each turn spitting out a little energy, none of it enough by itself, all of it added together just about sufficient to get him through the gate at seventh period.

activity: going on a first date
knowledge_domain: going on a first date
fact: A 2018 study by Erica Boothby and colleagues found a liking gap: after a first conversation, people usually underestimate how much the other person liked them and enjoyed their company.
story:
Naomi arrived at the theater eleven minutes early, which she decided was a manageable amount of early, and stood studying the poster for a documentary about deep-sea trawlers that neither of them had come to see. She and Bilal were seeing the horror film everyone in her grade had already seen twice. It had seemed, when he asked on Tuesday, like a safe choice: two hours in the dark, minimal talking, a shared adrenaline she could pretend was her own. Now, holding her ticket stub with its warm ink, she wondered whether choosing silence was a form of hiding, and whether hiding was dishonest, and whether dishonesty counted if the person you were hiding from had also chosen the dark.

He came through the glass doors shaking rain off his jacket, and the first thing he said was that he had almost bought the wrong popcorn, and then he had stood in front of the toppings for a full minute like an idiot. He told this as if it were a confession. Naomi said she had once spent an entire bus ride deciding between two kinds of gum, which was true, and he laughed in a way that seemed to surprise him, a short exhale, like the laugh had escaped before he approved it.

The trailers ran long. In the dark she became acutely aware of her own arms, of where her elbow rested on the shared armrest, of the fact that at some point their arms would either touch or not touch and both options felt enormous. When the monster finally appeared and the whole theater flinched, she flinched harder on purpose, and her shoulder knocked his, and he said "whoa" in a whisper, and neither of them moved away. It exhilarate her in a way the film itself did not, this small borrowed danger.

Afterward they stood under the awning while the rain decided what to do next. Bilal talked about the ending, about whether the sister had known all along, and Naomi argued the other side just to hear herself argue it, and she was good, she could feel herself being good, quick and funny, and then Jeffery from their calculus class came out of the late showing with two boys she didn't know and called across the lobby, "Bilal, my man, is this a date?" and everything in her chest dropped a floor.

Bilal said "we just saw a movie" at the exact moment Naomi said "kind of," and the two answers crossed in the air and neither of them looked at the other. Jeffery's group moved on toward the arcade games, hollering about something, and under the awning the rain went on being rain. Bilal put his hands in his pockets. Naomi said she should probably catch her bus, which was true in the sense that a bus existed.

She got a seat by the window and fell almost immediately into a reverie, but not the pleasant kind, a replaying kind. His "we just saw a movie" grew louder with each loop. She replayed the confession about the popcorn toppings, which now seemed pathetic rather than charming; the flinch, which now seemed staged; her arguments about the sister, which now seemed aggressive, the performance of a girl trying too hard to seem smart. By the time the bus crossed the river she had assembled the entire case, and the verdict felt axiomatic: he had spent two hours next to someone he regretted asking.

At her stop she found Jeffery's name in her phone before she had fully decided to use it. She typed, did you talk to bilal after? and then deleted it and typed, was that weird, what I said? and deleted that too. Finally she sent: his sister in that movie, did he think she knew? A minute passed, then two. The bus shelter's light buzzed above her. Jeffery replied: lol we argued about it the whole way to the arcade. he said you were funnier than the movie.
